logb(xy)=logbx+logbylogb(xk)=klogbxlogbx=lnxlnb=log10xlog10b\log_b(xy) = \log_b x + \log_b y \qquad \log_b(x^k) = k \log_b x \qquad \log_b x = \frac{\ln x}{\ln b} = \frac{\log_{10} x}{\log_{10} b}

Symbol Meaning Units
bb Base of the logarithm (b>0b > 0, b≠1b \neq 1) dimensionless
x,yx, y Positive numbers dimensionless
kk Any real exponent dimensionless
ln\ln Natural logarithm, base e≈2.71828e \approx 2.71828 —

The change-of-base rule means you only need one logarithm on your calculator. Two handy constants: log210≈3.32\log_2 10 \approx 3.32 and log102≈0.301\log_{10} 2 \approx 0.301.

Worked example — Binary search over one billion keys. How many comparisons does binary search need to find a key among n=109n = 10^9 sorted keys?

  1. We need log2(109)\log_2(10^9).
  2. Change of base: log2(109)=9×log210=9×3.32=29.9\log_2(10^9) = 9 \times \log_2 10 = 9 \times 3.32 = 29.9.
  3. Round up: 30 comparisons.

Interpretation. Thirty comparisons to search a billion items; a linear scan needs on average 500 million. Engineering implication. Each comparison in RAM costs on the order of 100 ns if it misses the CPU cache (§4.17), so 30 comparisons take roughly 3 µs. A sorted array or balanced tree in memory is fast enough for almost any lookup workload; the problem only becomes hard when each step requires a disk read, which is exactly the problem B-trees solve.

4.4.3 B-tree fan-out: why databases need only three or four disk reads

A binary tree halves the search space at each node, so a billion keys need about 30 levels. If each level is a random disk read, 30 reads is far too slow. A B-tree (detailed in §11.8 and §13.6) instead stores hundreds of keys per node, sized to fill one disk page, so each node splits the search space into hundreds of ranges [Bayer and McCreight 1972]. The number of children per node is the fan-out ff.

Height of a B-tree

h=⌈logfn⌉=⌈lognlogf⌉h = \left\lceil \log_f n \right\rceil = \left\lceil \frac{\log n}{\log f} \right\rceil

Symbol Meaning Units
hh Number of levels from root to leaf (page reads per lookup if nothing is cached) levels
nn Number of keys indexed keys
ff Fan-out: child pointers per internal node children/node
⌈⋅⌉\lceil \cdot \rceil Ceiling: round up to the next integer —

The derivation is the same counting argument as the paper folds: one root reaches ff children, which reach f2f^2 grandchildren, so hh levels reach fhf^h leaves. We need fh≥nf^h \geq n, so h≥logfnh \geq \log_f n.

Worked example — Fan-out of a 16 KiB page. A database uses 16 KiB pages (16,384 bytes). Each index entry in an internal node is an 8-byte key plus an 8-byte child pointer = 16 bytes. Assume 20% of each page goes to headers and free space. How tall is the index on 10910^9 keys?

  1. Usable bytes per page: 16,384×0.8=13,10716{,}384 \times 0.8 = 13{,}107 bytes.
  2. Fan-out: f=13,107/16≈819f = 13{,}107 / 16 \approx 819 children per node.
  3. Height: log819(109)=log10109log10819=92.913=3.09\log_{819}(10^9) = \dfrac{\log_{10} 10^9}{\log_{10} 819} = \dfrac{9}{2.913} = 3.09.
  4. Round up: h=4h = 4 levels.
  5. Compare: with f=1,000f = 1{,}000 the height would be exactly 9/3=39/3 = 3; a binary tree needs 30.

Interpretation. Four page reads locate any one of a billion keys. Engineering implication. The top two levels contain only 1+819=8201 + 819 = 820 pages, about 13 MiB, which fits easily in the buffer pool (§13.4). In practice a point lookup therefore costs one or two real I/Os, around 0.1–0.2 ms on an NVMe SSD (§4.17). Larger keys shrink fan-out: a 100-byte string key gives f≈13,107/108≈121f \approx 13{,}107/108 \approx 121 and h=⌈9/2.083⌉=5h = \lceil 9/2.083 \rceil = 5. Short keys are an index-design decision with measurable latency consequences.

Figure 4.1 — B-tree fan-out turns a billion keys into four levels.

Reading the diagram. Each rectangle is one fixed-size page. A lookup flows top-down synchronously: read the root, binary-search its keys in memory, follow one child pointer, repeat. The number of pages per level multiplies by the fan-out (1 → 819 → about 670,000 → leaves), so the count of levels grows only logarithmically. The Cached subgraph marks the storage boundary that matters: pages above it are in RAM and cost nanoseconds to microseconds, pages below it may require a disk read. The failure point is a cold cache after a restart, when every level costs an I/O. Scaling the data by another factor of 819 adds only one level.

Mistake — “Logarithmic means constant, so the base doesn’t matter.” Thirty dependent SSD reads at ~100 µs is 3 ms; four is 0.4 ms. The fan-out changes the constant by an order of magnitude.

4.5 Units: bits, bytes, rates and prefixes

4.5.1 Bits versus bytes

Definition — Bit and byte. A bit (symbol b) is a single binary digit, 0 or 1. A byte (symbol B) is 8 bits. Storage and memory are conventionally measured in bytes; network link speeds are conventionally measured in bits per second (bps).

The lowercase/uppercase distinction is load-bearing: 1 Gbps (gigabit per second) is one-eighth of 1 GB/s (gigabyte per second). Mixing them up produces an error of exactly 8×, which is large enough to invalidate a design and small enough to escape notice.

Converting link speed to byte throughput

RB/s=Rbps8ttransfer=8×SRbpsR_{\text{B/s}} = \frac{R_{\text{bps}}}{8} \qquad t_{\text{transfer}} = \frac{8 \times S}{R_{\text{bps}}}

Symbol Meaning Units
RbpsR_{\text{bps}} Link rate bits/second
RB/sR_{\text{B/s}} The same rate expressed in bytes bytes/second
SS Amount of data to transfer bytes
ttransfert_{\text{transfer}} Ideal transfer time, ignoring protocol overhead and congestion seconds

Worked example — Copying 1 TB across a 1 Gbps link.

  1. Convert data to bits: 1TB=10121\ \text{TB} = 10^{12} bytes =8×1012= 8 \times 10^{12} bits.
  2. Divide by the rate: 8×1012/109=8,0008 \times 10^{12} / 10^9 = 8{,}000 s.
  3. Convert to hours: 8,000/3,600≈2.28{,}000 / 3{,}600 \approx 2.2 h.
  4. At 10 Gbps: 800800 s ≈13\approx 13 min.

Interpretation. Even a “fast” link takes hours to move a terabyte; real transfers are slower because TCP/IP headers, TLS and congestion reduce goodput, commonly by 5–10% or more. Engineering implication. Rebuilding a failed 20 TB storage node over a single 10 Gbps link takes at least 8×2×1013/1010=16,0008 \times 2 \times 10^{13}/10^{10} = 16{,}000 s, about 4.4 hours. That repair window feeds directly into the durability calculations of §4.16, and it is why distributed stores spread re-replication across many source nodes in parallel.

4.5.2 SI versus binary prefixes

Two systems of prefixes coexist. The SI (decimal) prefixes k, M, G, T, P, E mean 103,106,109,…10^3, 10^6, 10^9, \ldots exactly. The binary prefixes Ki, Mi, Gi, Ti, Pi, Ei, standardized by the IEC (now in IEC 80000-13) [IEC 80000-13], mean 210,220,230,…2^{10}, 2^{20}, 2^{30}, \ldots exactly. Operating systems, memory vendors and disk vendors have historically used “GB” for both, which causes the classic “missing” capacity on a new drive.

Table 4.2 — SI versus binary prefixes.

SI name SI value Binary name Binary value Binary/SI ratio
kilobyte (KB or kB) 10310^3 kibibyte (KiB) 2102^{10} 1.024
megabyte (MB) 10610^6 mebibyte (MiB) 2202^{20} 1.049
gigabyte (GB) 10910^9 gibibyte (GiB) 2302^{30} 1.074
terabyte (TB) 101210^{12} tebibyte (TiB) 2402^{40} 1.100
petabyte (PB) 101510^{15} pebibyte (PiB) 2502^{50} 1.126
exabyte (EB) 101810^{18} exbibyte (EiB) 2602^{60} 1.153

Book convention. Following terminology.md, this book uses KB/MB/GB/TB = 10310^3/10610^6/10910^9/101210^{12} bytes for estimation and KiB/MiB/GiB when power-of-two precision matters (page sizes, memory allocation). Network rates are always decimal: 1 Gbps =109= 10^9 bits/s.

Worked example — The “missing” 7% on a new drive. A drive sold as 1 TB is shown by an operating system as “931 GB”.

  1. The vendor means SI: 101210^{12} bytes.
  2. The operating system divides by 2302^{30} but labels the result “GB”: 1012/1,073,741,824=931.310^{12} / 1{,}073{,}741{,}824 = 931.3.
  3. So the drive holds 931.3 GiB, and nothing is missing.

Interpretation. A 6.9% labeling discrepancy at the tera scale, growing to 12.6% at peta and 15.3% at exa. Engineering implication. In a capacity plan for 5 PB of data, confusing PB with PiB means under-provisioning by 5×0.126=0.635 \times 0.126 = 0.63 PB. State your units in every capacity document.

4.5.3 Rates and time conversions

Most capacity estimates start from a daily or monthly volume and must become a per-second rate, because servers are sized per second.

Table 4.3 — Time conversions used in estimation.

Period Seconds (exact) Handy approximation
1 minute 60 —
1 hour 3,600 3.6×1033.6 \times 10^3
1 day 86,400 ≈105\approx 10^5 (overestimates seconds by 16%)
1 week 604,800 ≈6×105\approx 6 \times 10^5
1 month (30 days) 2,592,000 ≈2.6×106\approx 2.6 \times 10^6
1 year (365 days) 31,536,000 ≈π×107\approx \pi \times 10^7

Average and peak rate from a daily volume

λ‾=Vday86,400λpeak=k×λ‾\bar{\lambda} = \frac{V_{\text{day}}}{86{,}400} \qquad \lambda_{\text{peak}} = k \times \bar{\lambda}

Symbol Meaning Units
VdayV_{\text{day}} Events (requests, writes, messages) per day events/day
λ‾\bar{\lambda} Average rate events/second
kk Peak-to-average ratio, measured or assumed (often 2–10 for consumer traffic) dimensionless
λpeak\lambda_{\text{peak}} Rate the system must be sized for events/second

Worked example — 100 million requests per day.

  1. Average: 108/86,400=1,15710^8 / 86{,}400 = 1{,}157 RPS.
  2. Shortcut check: 108/105=1,00010^8 / 10^5 = 1{,}000 RPS (16% low, acceptable for a first pass).
  3. Assume a peak-to-average ratio k=3k = 3: λpeak≈3,500\lambda_{\text{peak}} \approx 3{,}500 RPS.

Interpretation. “100 million a day” sounds enormous but is a few thousand requests per second at peak. Engineering implication. A few application servers can carry this request rate; the harder questions are usually storage growth and tail latency, not raw request rate. The peak factor kk is an assumption that must be stated and, once the system is live, measured.

4.6 Probability essentials

4.6.1 Probability, complement and independence

Definition — Probability. A number between 0 and 1 that measures how likely an event is: 0 means impossible, 1 means certain. If an experiment is repeated many times, the probability of event AA, written P(A)P(A), is the long-run fraction of repetitions in which AA happens.

First-principles explanation

Think of a fleet as a bag of marbles: if 1 in 1,000 is red, a blind draw is red with probability 0.001. Probability in system design is about the fleet: a disk with a 2% annual failure probability is rare on its own and a daily event among 100,000 disks.

Two rules carry most of the weight. The complement rule: P(not A)=1−P(A)P(\text{not } A) = 1 - P(A); computing “nothing goes wrong” is often far easier than enumerating what can. Independence: AA and BB are independent if knowing one happened tells you nothing about the other; then, and only then, P(A and B)=P(A)×P(B)P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \times P(B). Disks in different datacenters fail nearly independently; disks sharing a power supply do not.

Probability that at least one of NN independent components fails

P(at least one fails)=1−(1−p)NP(\text{at least one fails}) = 1 - (1 - p)^N

Symbol Meaning Units
pp Probability that a single component fails during the period of interest dimensionless (0–1)
NN Number of independent components count
(1−p)N(1-p)^N Probability that none fails (complement, multiplied NN times by independence) dimensionless

Derivation. One component survives with probability 1−p1 - p. By independence, all NN survive with probability (1−p)×(1−p)×⋯=(1−p)N(1-p)\times(1-p)\times\cdots = (1-p)^N. “At least one fails” is the complement of “all survive”. A useful approximation for small pp: (1−p)N≈e−Np(1-p)^N \approx e^{-Np}, so P(at least one)≈1−e−NpP(\text{at least one}) \approx 1 - e^{-Np}, and when Np≪1Np \ll 1 this is simply ≈Np\approx Np.

Worked example — At least one of 1,000 servers fails today. Each server independently fails on a given day with probability p=0.001p = 0.001 (one failure per thousand server-days). The fleet has N=1,000N = 1{,}000 servers.

  1. Probability one server survives the day: 1−0.001=0.9991 - 0.001 = 0.999.
  2. Probability all survive: 0.99910000.999^{1000}. Using the approximation: e−1000×0.001=e−1=0.368e^{-1000 \times 0.001} = e^{-1} = 0.368. (Exact: 0.3677.)
  3. Probability at least one fails: 1−0.368=0.6321 - 0.368 = 0.632.

Interpretation. A component that almost never fails individually produces a failure on 63% of days at fleet scale. At N=10,000N = 10{,}000 the probability is 1−e−10>0.99991 - e^{-10} > 0.9999: a failure every day. Engineering implication. At scale, failure is not an exception to handle but a steady background rate to design for. This is the quantitative core of “design for failure” (§2.9): automation must detect and replace failed nodes without human intervention, because humans cannot be paged every day for routine events.

4.6.2 Union and intersection

Union (inclusion–exclusion) and intersection

P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B)P(A∩B)=P(A)×P(B∣A)P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B) \qquad P(A \cap B) = P(A) \times P(B \mid A)

Symbol Meaning Units
P(A∪B)P(A \cup B) Probability that AA or BB (or both) happens dimensionless
P(A∩B)P(A \cap B) Probability that both happen dimensionless
P(B∣A)P(B \mid A) Conditional probability of BB given that AA happened; equals P(B)P(B) when independent dimensionless

The subtraction in the union rule avoids counting “both” twice. The conditional form of the intersection rule is how correlation enters: if two replicas share a rack, P(B∣A)P(B \mid A) — the probability that the second fails given that the first did — can be many times larger than P(B)P(B).

Worked example — Two dependencies, independent versus correlated. A request needs both a cache and a database. On a given day, the cache has an outage with probability 0.01 and the database with probability 0.02.

  1. If independent: P(both)=0.01×0.02=0.0002P(\text{both}) = 0.01 \times 0.02 = 0.0002.
  2. P(either)=0.01+0.02−0.0002=0.0298P(\text{either}) = 0.01 + 0.02 - 0.0002 = 0.0298.
  3. Now suppose they share a network switch, so that given a cache outage the database is also out with probability 0.5: P(both)=0.01×0.5=0.005P(\text{both}) = 0.01 \times 0.5 = 0.005 — 25 times the independent value.

Interpretation. The probability of “something breaks” barely changes, but the probability of “both break together” rises 25×. Engineering implication. Redundancy arithmetic (§4.14, §4.16) assumes independence. Every shared dependency — a rack, a power feed, a software version, a configuration push — breaks that assumption, which is why real systems spread replicas across failure domains.

4.6.3 Expected value

Definition — Expected value. The probability-weighted average outcome of a random quantity XX: E[X]=∑ixiP(X=xi)E[X] = \sum_i x_i \, P(X = x_i). It is the long-run average over many repetitions.

Expected value and linearity of expectation

E[X]=∑ixiP(X=xi)E[X1+X2+⋯+XN]=E[X1]+⋯+E[XN]E[X] = \sum_i x_i\,P(X = x_i) \qquad E[X_1 + X_2 + \cdots + X_N] = E[X_1] + \cdots + E[X_N]

Symbol Meaning Units
XX A random quantity (failures, latency, cost) units of the quantity
xix_i A possible value of XX units of the quantity
P(X=xi)P(X = x_i) Probability of that value dimensionless

Linearity is powerful because it holds even when the components are not independent. The expected number of failed servers is N×pN \times p whatever the correlation.

Worked example — Expected cost of a retry policy. A call fails with probability 0.05 and is retried once on failure. What is the expected number of calls per request?

  1. Outcomes: 1 call with probability 0.95; 2 calls with probability 0.05.
  2. E[calls]=1×0.95+2×0.05=0.95+0.10=1.05E[\text{calls}] = 1 \times 0.95 + 2 \times 0.05 = 0.95 + 0.10 = 1.05.

Interpretation. Retries add 5% load in normal operation. But if a dependency is degraded so that 50% of calls fail, the same policy gives 1×0.5+2×0.5=1.51 \times 0.5 + 2 \times 0.5 = 1.5 calls per request — a 50% load increase on the struggling dependency. Engineering implication. Retries amplify load precisely when the system is weakest. Retry budgets (§22.12) cap this expected amplification.

4.6.4 The binomial distribution

When there are NN independent trials, each “failing” with probability pp, the number of failures KK follows a binomial distribution.

Binomial probability of exactly kk failures

P(K=k)=(Nk)pk(1−p)N−k,(Nk)=N!k!(N−k)!,E[K]=NpP(K = k) = \binom{N}{k} p^k (1-p)^{N-k}, \qquad \binom{N}{k} = \frac{N!}{k!\,(N-k)!}, \qquad E[K] = Np

Symbol Meaning Units
NN Number of independent components (trials) count
kk Number of failures we ask about count
pp Per-component failure probability in the period dimensionless
(Nk)\binom{N}{k} Number of ways to choose which kk components fail (“NN choose kk”) count
E[K]E[K] Expected number of failures count

Derivation. One specific set of kk failures and N−kN-k survivals has probability pk(1−p)N−kp^k(1-p)^{N-k} by independence. There are (Nk)\binom{N}{k} such sets, and they are mutually exclusive, so we add them.

Worked example — How many spare servers are enough? Continuing the fleet of N=1,000N = 1{,}000 servers with daily failure probability p=0.001p = 0.001:

  1. Expected failures per day: E[K]=1000×0.001=1E[K] = 1000 \times 0.001 = 1.
  2. P(K=0)=0.9991000=0.3677P(K = 0) = 0.999^{1000} = 0.3677.
  3. P(K=1)=1000×0.001×0.999999=0.3681P(K = 1) = 1000 \times 0.001 \times 0.999^{999} = 0.3681.
  4. P(K=2)=(10002)×0.0012×0.999998=499,500×10−6×0.3685=0.1840P(K = 2) = \binom{1000}{2} \times 0.001^2 \times 0.999^{998} = 499{,}500 \times 10^{-6} \times 0.3685 = 0.1840.
  5. P(K≥3)=1−0.3677−0.3681−0.1840=0.0802P(K \geq 3) = 1 - 0.3677 - 0.3681 - 0.1840 = 0.0802.

Interpretation. On about 8% of days — roughly 29 days per year — three or more servers fail. Engineering implication. Provisioning spare capacity for “the average day” (one failure) leaves you short on one day in twelve. Capacity headroom should be chosen against a percentile of the failure distribution, not its mean.

4.7 Statistics: describing measurements

Probability reasons forward from a model to predictions. Statistics reasons backward from measurements (latency samples, failure logs) to a description of what is happening.

4.7.1 Mean and median

Definition — Mean and median. The mean (arithmetic average) of nn values is their sum divided by nn. The median is the middle value after sorting (the average of the two middle values when nn is even); half of the values are at or below it.

First-principles explanation

If nine people in a café each earn 50,000 a year and a billionaire walks in, the mean income in the room jumps to over 100 million while the median does not move. The mean is sensitive to every value, including extreme ones; the median is sensitive only to rank. Latency data behave like the café: most requests are quick, a few are extremely slow, and the slow ones drag the mean.

Mean, variance and standard deviation

x‾=1n∑i=1nxiσ2=1n∑i=1n(xi−x‾)2σ=σ2\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i \qquad \sigma^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i - \bar{x})^2 \qquad \sigma = \sqrt{\sigma^2}

Symbol Meaning Units
xix_i The ii-th measurement e.g. ms
nn Number of measurements count
x‾\bar{x} Mean same as xx (ms)
σ2\sigma^2 Variance: average squared distance from the mean ms²
σ\sigma Standard deviation: typical distance from the mean ms

This is the population variance (divide by nn). When estimating the variance of a larger population from a sample, statisticians divide by n−1n - 1 instead (the sample variance); for the large samples typical of latency monitoring the difference is negligible.

Worked example — Ten latency measurements with one outlier. Measured latencies in ms: 12, 15, 11, 14, 13, 16, 12, 18, 14, 250.

  1. Sum: 12+15+11+14+13+16+12+18+14+250=37512+15+11+14+13+16+12+18+14+250 = 375. Mean: 375/10=37.5375/10 = 37.5 ms.
  2. Sorted: 11, 12, 12, 13, 14, 14, 15, 16, 18, 250. Median: average of 5th and 6th values =(14+14)/2=14= (14 + 14)/2 = 14 ms.
  3. Squared deviations from 37.5: (12−37.5)2=650.25(12-37.5)^2 = 650.25; similarly 506.25, 702.25, 552.25, 600.25, 462.25, 650.25, 380.25, 552.25, and (250−37.5)2=45,156.25(250-37.5)^2 = 45{,}156.25. Sum =50,212.5= 50{,}212.5.
  4. Variance: 50,212.5/10=5,021.2550{,}212.5 / 10 = 5{,}021.25 ms². Standard deviation: 5021.25=70.9\sqrt{5021.25} = 70.9 ms.
  5. Without the outlier: mean 13.9 ms, median 14 ms, standard deviation 2.1 ms.

Interpretation. One slow request in ten makes the mean 2.7 times the median and inflates the standard deviation 34-fold. The mean (37.5 ms) describes no actual request: nine were under 20 ms and one was 250 ms. Engineering implication. Report latency as percentiles (§4.8), not as mean ± standard deviation. Mean and standard deviation summarize a distribution well only when it is roughly symmetric and thin-tailed, which latency almost never is.

4.7.2 Distributions: normal, exponential, log-normal and Pareto

A probability distribution describes how likely each value is. Four shapes cover most of what you will meet.

The normal (Gaussian) distribution is the symmetric bell curve. It arises when many small independent effects add up. About 68% of values lie within 1σ1\sigma of the mean, 95% within 2σ2\sigma and 99.7% within 3σ3\sigma. Extreme values are vanishingly rare: a 6σ6\sigma event has probability around 10−910^{-9}.

The exponential distribution describes the time between independent random events occurring at a constant average rate λ\lambda, such as request arrivals from many independent users, or failures of a component that does not age. Its mean is 1/λ1/\lambda and P(T>t)=e−λtP(T > t) = e^{-\lambda t}. It is memoryless: having waited 5 seconds tells you nothing about how much longer you will wait. It underpins queueing theory (§4.10) and reliability theory (§4.15).

The log-normal distribution describes a quantity whose logarithm is normal — the result of many small multiplicative effects. Request latency often looks roughly log-normal: a long right tail, with the mean above the median. If lnX\ln X has mean μ\mu and standard deviation ss, then the median of XX is eμe^{\mu} and the mean is eμ+s2/2e^{\mu + s^2/2}.

The Pareto (power-law) distribution has P(X>x)=(xm/x)αP(X > x) = (x_m / x)^{\alpha} for x≥xmx \geq x_m. Its tail decays polynomially, not exponentially, so extreme values are far more common than a normal model predicts. File sizes, object popularity, and per-user activity are frequently described as heavy-tailed (Harchol-Balter 2013 discusses heavy-tailed job sizes in depth). With α≈1.16\alpha \approx 1.16 you get the “80/20 rule”: the top 20% of items account for 80% of the total. For α≤1\alpha \leq 1 the mean is infinite; for α≤2\alpha \leq 2 the variance is infinite, so sample averages never settle down.

Tail formulas for three skewed distributions

Exponential: P(T>t)=e−λt,E[T]=1λLog-normal: median=eμ,mean=eμ+s2/2Pareto: P(X>x)=(xmx)α\text{Exponential: } P(T > t) = e^{-\lambda t},\ E[T] = \frac{1}{\lambda} \qquad \text{Log-normal: median} = e^{\mu},\ \text{mean} = e^{\mu + s^2/2} \qquad \text{Pareto: } P(X > x) = \left(\frac{x_m}{x}\right)^{\alpha}

Symbol Meaning Units
λ\lambda Event rate of the exponential distribution events/second
tt Elapsed time seconds
μ,s\mu, s Mean and standard deviation of lnX\ln X for a log-normal XX ln of the unit of XX
xmx_m Pareto minimum (scale) value unit of XX (e.g. bytes)
α\alpha Pareto tail index: smaller means heavier tail dimensionless

Table 4.4 — Four distributions and where they appear in systems.

Distribution Shape Tail Typical system quantity Mean vs median
Normal Symmetric bell Very thin (e−x2e^{-x^2}) Aggregates of many small effects; measurement noise Equal
Exponential Decaying from zero Thin (e−xe^{-x}) Inter-arrival times; failures of non-aging parts Mean ≈ 1.44 × median
Log-normal Right-skewed Moderately heavy Request latency, service times Mean > median
Pareto Right-skewed, power law Heavy (polynomial) File sizes, key popularity, user activity Mean ≫ median (may be infinite)

Worked example — Mean versus median for a log-normal latency. Suppose ln(latency in ms)\ln(\text{latency in ms}) has mean μ=ln20=2.996\mu = \ln 20 = 2.996 and standard deviation s=1.0s = 1.0.

  1. Median: eμ=20e^{\mu} = 20 ms.
  2. Mean: eμ+s2/2=e2.996+0.5=20×e0.5=20×1.649=33.0e^{\mu + s^2/2} = e^{2.996 + 0.5} = 20 \times e^{0.5} = 20 \times 1.649 = 33.0 ms.
  3. The 99th percentile of a normal variable is μ+2.326s\mu + 2.326\,s, so p99 =e2.996+2.326=20×e2.326=20×10.24=205= e^{2.996 + 2.326} = 20 \times e^{2.326} = 20 \times 10.24 = 205 ms.

Interpretation. The p99 is about 10 times the median, and the mean sits 65% above the median. Engineering implication. If you set a timeout at the mean (33 ms) you will time out nearly one request in three: ln33−ln20=0.50\ln 33 - \ln 20 = 0.50, which is 0.5s0.5\,s above μ\mu, and a normal variable exceeds μ+0.5s\mu + 0.5\,s with probability 0.31. The Python example in §4.8.2 samples this exact distribution and confirms these values empirically.

4.7.3 Why averages lie

Averages mislead in four recurring ways: skew (the mean is pulled toward the tail, as above); time aggregation (a day-long average of 50 ms can hide a 10-minute window at 2 s); averaging percentiles (a fleet p99 is not the mean of per-host p99s — merge histograms instead, §4.8.3); and averaging over users (if 1% of users send 50% of requests, per-request and per-user averages can tell opposite stories).

Mistake — “Average latency is 40 ms, so we meet our 100 ms SLO.” An SLO is about the fraction of requests that are fast enough. A mean of 40 ms is compatible with 10% of requests taking over a second. SLOs are written in percentiles (§39.6) for exactly this reason.

4.8 Percentiles and tail latency

4.8.1 Definition

Definition — Percentile. The qq-th percentile of a set of measurements is the value at or below which qq% of the measurements fall. Latency percentiles are written p50 (the median), p95, p99 and p99.9 (also written p999): the 50th, 95th, 99th and 99.9th percentiles.

First-principles explanation

Line up 1,000 runners by finishing time: the p50 is the 500th runner’s time, the p99 the 990th’s, the p99.9 the 999th’s. Percentiles describe what a fraction of requests experiences — if your p99 is 2 s, one request in a hundred is painfully slow, and a page making 50 requests will often hit one (§4.8.4).

The region above roughly p99 is called the tail, and tail latency is the study of why those requests are slow and how to make them faster. Causes include garbage-collection pauses, queueing behind a large request, background compaction, cache misses, retransmitted packets and noisy neighbors [Dean and Barroso 2013].

4.8.2 Computing percentiles from samples

The simplest definition is the nearest-rank method.

Nearest-rank percentile

r=⌈q100×n⌉,pq=x(r)r = \left\lceil \frac{q}{100} \times n \right\rceil, \qquad \text{p}q = x_{(r)}

Symbol Meaning Units
qq Desired percentile, 0<q≤1000 < q \leq 100 percent
nn Number of samples count
rr 1-based rank in the sorted list position
x(r)x_{(r)} The rr-th smallest sample e.g. ms

Other definitions interpolate between neighboring samples (NumPy’s default does); they differ noticeably only when nn is small. With 10 samples, a “p99” is just the maximum, which is why a p99 needs at least several hundred samples and a p99.9 several thousand to mean anything.

Worked example — Percentiles of the ten measurements from §4.7.1. Sorted: 11, 12, 12, 13, 14, 14, 15, 16, 18, 250.

  1. p50: r=⌈0.50×10⌉=5r = \lceil 0.50 \times 10 \rceil = 5 → 14 ms.
  2. p90: r=⌈0.90×10⌉=9r = \lceil 0.90 \times 10 \rceil = 9 → 18 ms.
  3. p95: r=⌈0.95×10⌉=⌈9.5⌉=10r = \lceil 0.95 \times 10 \rceil = \lceil 9.5 \rceil = 10 → 250 ms.

Interpretation. p90 and p95 differ by a factor of 14 because with ten samples they land on different single observations. Engineering implication. Always report the sample count alongside a high percentile, and alert on percentiles computed over windows large enough to contain hundreds of tail samples.

The following program samples the log-normal distribution of §4.7.2, computes percentiles, and then checks the fan-out formula of §4.8.4 by simulation.

import math
import random
import statistics

def percentile_nearest_rank(samples, p):
    """Return the p-th percentile (0 < p <= 100) using the nearest-rank method."""
    if not samples:
        raise ValueError("no samples")
    ordered = sorted(samples)
    rank = math.ceil(p / 100 * len(ordered))   # 1-based rank
    return ordered[max(rank, 1) - 1]

random.seed(42)
# Log-normal latencies: median ~20 ms, heavy right tail (sigma = 1.0)
latencies_ms = [random.lognormvariate(math.log(20), 1.0) for _ in range(100_000)]

print(f"mean   = {statistics.fmean(latencies_ms):7.1f} ms")
for p in (50, 90, 99, 99.9):
    print(f"p{p:<5} = {percentile_nearest_rank(latencies_ms, p):7.1f} ms")

# Fan-out: a request waits for the slowest of N parallel calls
p99 = percentile_nearest_rank(latencies_ms, 99)
for n in (1, 10, 100):
    trials = 20_000
    slow = sum(
        max(random.choice(latencies_ms) for _ in range(n)) > p99
        for _ in range(trials)
    )
    print(f"N={n:>3}: simulated P(slow) = {slow/trials:.3f}, "
          f"formula 1 - 0.99^N = {1 - 0.99**n:.3f}")

Output (Python 3.13):

mean   =    32.9 ms
p50    =    20.0 ms
p90    =    72.2 ms
p99    =   201.3 ms
p99.9  =   428.4 ms
N=  1: simulated P(slow) = 0.010, formula 1 - 0.99^N = 0.010
N= 10: simulated P(slow) = 0.093, formula 1 - 0.99^N = 0.096
N=100: simulated P(slow) = 0.637, formula 1 - 0.99^N = 0.634

What to notice:

  • The simulated mean (32.9 ms), median (20.0 ms) and p99 (201 ms) match the closed-form values of §4.7.2 (33.0, 20 and 205 ms) within sampling error.
  • max(...) models a request that must wait for all of its parallel sub-requests; the simulated probability of exceeding the single-server p99 matches 1−0.99N1 - 0.99^N.
  • Sorting 100,000 samples is fine offline, but production systems cannot keep every sample; they use histograms.

4.8.3 Histograms

A histogram counts how many samples fall into each of a fixed set of buckets. It uses constant memory regardless of request volume, and two histograms with identical buckets can be merged by adding counts, which makes fleet-wide percentiles possible. Percentiles are read from the cumulative counts, with an error no larger than the bucket width. Libraries such as HdrHistogram use buckets whose width grows with the value (logarithmic or log-linear buckets) so that relative error stays bounded across many orders of magnitude [Tene, HdrHistogram].

Worked example — p99 and p99.9 from a histogram. 10,000 requests are counted into buckets (ms): [0,10): 6,000; [10,20): 2,500; [20,50): 1,000; [50,100): 350; [100,200): 120; [200,500): 25; [500,1000): 5.

  1. Cumulative counts: 6,000; 8,500; 9,500; 9,850; 9,970; 9,995; 10,000.
  2. p99 is rank 0.99×10,000=9,9000.99 \times 10{,}000 = 9{,}900. The cumulative count first reaches 9,900 in the [100,200) bucket (9,850 → 9,970).
  3. Interpolate linearly inside the bucket: (9,900−9,850)/120=0.417(9{,}900 - 9{,}850)/120 = 0.417 of the way through, so p99 ≈100+0.417×100=142\approx 100 + 0.417 \times 100 = 142 ms.
  4. p99.9 is rank 9,990, inside [200,500) (9,970 → 9,995): (9,990−9,970)/25=0.8(9{,}990 - 9{,}970)/25 = 0.8, so p99.9 ≈200+0.8×300=440\approx 200 + 0.8 \times 300 = 440 ms.

Interpretation. The true p99 is somewhere in [100, 200) ms; interpolation assumes samples are spread evenly inside the bucket. Engineering implication. Bucket boundaries should be densest where your SLO thresholds lie. If the SLO is “p99 < 150 ms”, a bucket edge exactly at 150 ms lets you count SLO violations exactly rather than estimate them.

4.8.4 Fan-out amplification

Modern requests are rarely served by one machine. A search query may be scattered to hundreds of index partitions (§16.7); a page render may call dozens of microservices. If a request must wait for all of its NN sub-requests, then it is slow whenever any of them is slow.

Figure 4.2 — Fan-out: the slowest leaf determines the response time.

Reading the diagram. The client sends one HTTPS request to a root service, which issues NN parallel RPCs to leaf services, each owning one data partition (the cylinders mark storage boundaries). All arrows are synchronous request/response except the dotted arrow, which highlights the one leaf whose reply arrives late. The root cannot answer until every leaf replies (or a deadline fires), so the response time is the maximum of NN leaf latencies. Every leaf is a failure point for the whole request. Scaling out by adding partitions increases NN and therefore makes the tail worse unless tail-tolerant techniques are used.

Probability that a fan-out request is fast

P(all N fast)=pNP(at least one slow)=1−pNprequired=Ptarget1/NP(\text{all } N \text{ fast}) = p^N \qquad P(\text{at least one slow}) = 1 - p^N \qquad p_{\text{required}} = P_{\text{target}}^{1/N}

Symbol Meaning Units
pp Probability that one leaf responds within the threshold (e.g. 0.99 at the leaf’s p99) dimensionless
NN Number of parallel sub-requests the root must wait for count
PtargetP_{\text{target}} Desired probability that the whole request is fast dimensionless
prequiredp_{\text{required}} Per-leaf probability needed to meet PtargetP_{\text{target}} dimensionless

This is the complement rule of §4.6.1 again, assuming leaf latencies are independent.

Worked example — 100-way fan-out. Each leaf answers within 10 ms with probability 0.99 (its p99 is 10 ms). The root fans out to N=100N = 100 leaves.

  1. P(all fast)=0.99100=0.366P(\text{all fast}) = 0.99^{100} = 0.366.
  2. P(at least one slow)=1−0.366=0.634P(\text{at least one slow}) = 1 - 0.366 = 0.634.
  3. For 99% of root requests to be fast we need p=0.991/100=0.99990p = 0.99^{1/100} = 0.99990: every leaf must meet the 10 ms threshold at its p99.99.
  4. With N=10N = 10: 0.9910=0.9040.99^{10} = 0.904, so 9.6% of requests are slow.

Interpretation. A leaf p99 becomes the root’s p37 or so: 63% of user requests see at least one slow leaf. This is the example Dean and Barroso use to open The Tail at Scale: with a one-in-a-hundred chance of a slow leaf, 63% of 100-way fan-out requests are slow [Dean and Barroso 2013]. Engineering implication. In fan-out architectures you must engineer the leaf p99.9 or p99.99, not the leaf p99, or use tail-tolerant techniques that break the pNp^N law.

Real-world industry applications

Google — tail-tolerant techniques. Dean and Barroso describe how large fan-out services at Google tolerate latency variability instead of trying to eliminate it. Hedged requests send a second copy of a request to another replica if the first has not answered within, for example, the 95th-percentile expected latency, and use whichever reply arrives first; tied requests enqueue the request on two servers and let the first to start cancel the other. They report a benchmark reading 1,000 keys from 100 BigTable servers in which hedging after 10 ms cut the p99.9 latency from 1,800 ms to 74 ms while sending only about 2% more requests. Trade-off: hedging spends a little extra load to cut the tail, and must be disabled or rate-limited under overload so it does not amplify it. Chapter 23 (§23.6–§23.7) covers implementation. Evidence: Primary — [Dean and Barroso 2013]

Two further traps are covered in Chapter 23: computing a fleet p99 by averaging per-host p99s (merge histograms instead, §4.8.3), and coordinated omission, where a load generator that waits for slow replies stops sending during slow periods and so under-samples the tail (§23.5).

Mistake — “Our p99 is fine, so only 1% of users suffer.” If a user session issues 100 requests, the probability that the session contains at least one request slower than p99 is 1−0.99100=63%1 - 0.99^{100} = 63\%. Percentiles are per request; user experience is per session.

4.9 Basic linear algebra

This section is a preparation for the ML chapters (Part XI onward), where embeddings, similarity search and matrix multiplication dominate cost. You need only three ideas: vectors, the dot product and matrix multiplication.

4.9.1 Vectors

Definition — Vector. An ordered list of dd numbers, 𝐚=(a1,a2,…,ad)\mathbf{a} = (a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_d), where dd is the dimension. Geometrically, a vector is an arrow from the origin to a point in dd-dimensional space; its length (or norm) is ∥𝐚∥=a12+⋯+ad2\lVert \mathbf{a} \rVert = \sqrt{a_1^2 + \cdots + a_d^2}.

First-principles explanation

A map location is a 2-dimensional vector (latitude, longitude); a song might be a 3-dimensional vector (tempo, loudness, acousticness). An ML embedding is the same idea with hundreds or thousands of learned dimensions, arranged so that similar items point in similar directions. “Find similar items” becomes “find nearby arrows” (Chapter 74).

4.9.2 Dot product and cosine similarity

Dot product and cosine similarity

𝐚⋅𝐛=∑i=1daibicosθ=𝐚⋅𝐛∥𝐚∥∥𝐛∥\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = \sum_{i=1}^{d} a_i b_i \qquad \cos\theta = \frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{\lVert \mathbf{a} \rVert\,\lVert \mathbf{b} \rVert}

Symbol Meaning Units
𝐚,𝐛\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} Two vectors of the same dimension (embedding units; dimensionless)
dd Dimension count
ai,bia_i, b_i ii-th components dimensionless
∥𝐚∥\lVert \mathbf{a} \rVert Length of 𝐚\mathbf{a} dimensionless
θ\theta Angle between the vectors radians or degrees
cosθ\cos\theta Cosine similarity: 1 = same direction, 0 = unrelated (perpendicular), −1 = opposite dimensionless

The dot product multiplies matching components and adds the results. Dividing by both lengths removes the effect of magnitude, so cosine similarity measures direction only. If vectors are normalized to length 1 in advance (common for embeddings), cosine similarity is the dot product, which is cheaper to compute.

Worked example — Which document is closest to the query? Query 𝐪=(1,2,2)\mathbf{q} = (1, 2, 2); document 𝐚=(2,1,2)\mathbf{a} = (2, 1, 2); document 𝐛=(2,4,4)\mathbf{b} = (2, 4, 4).

  1. 𝐪⋅𝐚=1×2+2×1+2×2=2+2+4=8\mathbf{q} \cdot \mathbf{a} = 1 \times 2 + 2 \times 1 + 2 \times 2 = 2 + 2 + 4 = 8.
  2. ∥𝐪∥=1+4+4=3\lVert \mathbf{q} \rVert = \sqrt{1 + 4 + 4} = 3; ∥𝐚∥=4+1+4=3\lVert \mathbf{a} \rVert = \sqrt{4 + 1 + 4} = 3.
  3. cosθqa=8/(3×3)=0.889\cos\theta_{qa} = 8 / (3 \times 3) = 0.889 (an angle of about 27°).
  4. 𝐪⋅𝐛=2+8+8=18\mathbf{q} \cdot \mathbf{b} = 2 + 8 + 8 = 18; ∥𝐛∥=4+16+16=6\lVert \mathbf{b} \rVert = \sqrt{4 + 16 + 16} = 6; cosθqb=18/(3×6)=1.0\cos\theta_{qb} = 18 / (3 \times 6) = 1.0.

Interpretation. 𝐛\mathbf{b} is exactly twice 𝐪\mathbf{q}, so it points the same way: cosine 1.0. The raw dot product (18 vs 8) also prefers 𝐛\mathbf{b} but would be fooled by long vectors in general. Engineering implication. Choose the similarity metric the embedding model was trained with; normalize vectors once at ingestion so that serving-time similarity is a plain dot product.

4.9.3 Matrices and the cost of matrix multiplication

Definition — Matrix. A rectangular grid of numbers with mm rows and nn columns (an m×nm \times n matrix). A set of nn embeddings of dimension dd is naturally stored as an n×dn \times d matrix, one embedding per row.

Multiplying an m×km \times k matrix AA by a k×nk \times n matrix BB produces an m×nm \times n matrix CC in which each entry CijC_{ij} is the dot product of row ii of AA with column jj of BB. Each of the m×nm \times n entries is a dot product of length kk.

Cost of matrix multiplication

FLOPs=2mnkarithmetic intensity=FLOPsbytes moved\text{FLOPs} = 2\,m\,n\,k \qquad \text{arithmetic intensity} = \frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{bytes moved}}

Symbol Meaning Units
m,km, k Rows and columns of AA count
k,nk, n Rows and columns of BB (inner dimension kk must match) count
FLOPs Floating-point operations: one multiply and one add per term operations
bytes moved Data read from and written to memory bytes
arithmetic intensity FLOPs per byte; low values mean memory-bandwidth-bound, high values compute-bound FLOP/byte

Worked example — Brute-force similarity search and the value of batching.

Part A: one query against one million embeddings. n=106n = 10^6 embeddings of dimension d=768d = 768 stored as 4-byte floats.

  1. Storage: 106×768×4=3.07×10910^6 \times 768 \times 4 = 3.07 \times 10^9 bytes ≈ 3.1 GB.
  2. Compute: one dot product per embedding, 106×768=7.68×10810^6 \times 768 = 7.68 \times 10^8 multiply-adds = 1.54×1091.54 \times 10^9 FLOPs.
  3. Intensity: 1.54×109/3.07×109=0.51.54 \times 10^9 / 3.07 \times 10^9 = 0.5 FLOP/byte — every float is loaded once and used once.
  4. If memory delivers 20 GB/s to this computation (an illustrative figure), scanning takes 3.07/20=0.153.07 / 20 = 0.15 s per query, regardless of how fast the arithmetic is.

Part B: a neural-network layer. Multiply a batch of mm inputs (m×4096m \times 4096) by a 4096×40964096 \times 4096 weight matrix stored in 2-byte (16-bit) floats.

  1. Weights: 4096×4096×2=33.54096 \times 4096 \times 2 = 33.5 MB.
  2. With m=1m = 1: FLOPs =2×1×4096×4096=3.36×107= 2 \times 1 \times 4096 \times 4096 = 3.36 \times 10^7, intensity ≈ 3.36×107/3.36×107=13.36 \times 10^7 / 3.36 \times 10^7 = 1 FLOP/byte.
  3. With m=32m = 32: FLOPs =2×32×4096×4096=1.07×109= 2 \times 32 \times 4096 \times 4096 = 1.07 \times 10^9; the weights are read once for the whole batch, so intensity ≈ 32 FLOP/byte.

Interpretation. Brute-force search and single-request inference are memory-bound: the processor waits for data. Batching reuses each loaded weight for many inputs and raises arithmetic intensity proportionally. Engineering implication. At a million vectors and many queries per second, brute force is too slow, which motivates approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) indexes (Chapter 74). For model serving, batching is the main lever for throughput — at a latency cost quantified in §4.18.6.

import math

def dot(a, b):
    return sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b, strict=True))

def norm(a):
    return math.sqrt(dot(a, a))

def cosine_similarity(a, b):
    return dot(a, b) / (norm(a) * norm(b))

def matmul(A, B):
    """Naive matrix multiply: (m x k) times (k x n) -> (m x n)."""
    m, k, n = len(A), len(B), len(B[0])
    assert all(len(row) == k for row in A), "inner dimensions must match"
    return [[sum(A[i][t] * B[t][j] for t in range(k)) for j in range(n)]
            for i in range(m)]

query = [1, 2, 2]
docs = {"doc_a": [2, 1, 2], "doc_b": [2, 4, 4], "doc_c": [-2, 1, 0]}
for name, vec in docs.items():
    print(f"{name}: dot = {dot(query, vec):3d}, cosine = {cosine_similarity(query, vec):.3f}")

# Score all documents at once: (1 x 3) query times (3 x 3) matrix of doc columns
D = [list(col) for col in zip(*docs.values())]   # 3 x 3, one document per column
print("scores via matmul:", matmul([query], D)[0])

Output:

doc_a: dot =   8, cosine = 0.889
doc_b: dot =  18, cosine = 1.000
doc_c: dot =   0, cosine = 0.000
scores via matmul: [8, 18, 0]

What to notice:

  • zip(..., strict=True) (Python 3.10+) raises an error if dimensions differ, a cheap guard against mixing embeddings from different models.
  • doc_c is perpendicular to the query (dot product 0): unrelated, not opposite.
  • Scoring many documents is one matrix multiplication. The triple loop in matmul performs exactly m×n×km \times n \times k multiply-adds; production libraries (BLAS, GPU kernels) do the same arithmetic but reorganize it to reuse data in caches.

4.10 Queueing theory

4.10.1 Vocabulary

Definition — Queueing system. A model in which jobs (requests, messages, packets) arrive at a service center, wait in a queue if all servers are busy, receive service, and depart. The arrival rate λ\lambda is the average number of jobs arriving per second; the service rate μ\mu is the average number of jobs one server can complete per second when it is never idle, so the average service time is S=1/μS = 1/\mu.

First-principles explanation

Picture a supermarket checkout. Customers arrive at random and take a random time to serve. When the cashier is idle half the time, a queue rarely forms; when the cashier is busy 95% of the time, a long queue is routine, although the cashier is not technically overloaded. Waiting is caused by variability, and its effect grows without bound as utilization approaches 100%. With perfectly regular arrivals and service, a cashier at 99% would never have a queue. Every CPU core, disk, thread, connection and network link in a design is a checkout.

Why does this exist?

Capacity plans that ignore queueing assume a server at 90% utilization performs like one at 50%. It does not. Queueing theory, begun by Erlang for telephone exchanges and developed for computer systems from the 1960s onward [Kleinrock 1975; Harchol-Balter 2013], quantifies how much worse it is.

Kendall notation names queue models as A/S/c: arrival process / service-time distribution / number of servers. “M” stands for Markovian (memoryless): Poisson arrivals, meaning exponentially distributed gaps between arrivals (§4.7.2), or exponentially distributed service times. M/M/1 is the simplest model: random arrivals, random service, one server, first-come-first-served, unlimited queue.

4.10.2 The M/M/1 queue

Figure 4.3 — The M/M/1 queue.

Reading the diagram. Jobs flow left to right. Arrivals come from many independent clients at average rate λ\lambda (requests/s); the queue (subroutine shape) is a buffer, typically in memory, with no limit in this model; the single server processes one job at a time at average rate μ\mu. In steady state, departures equal arrivals (λ\lambda), so throughput is set by demand, not by the server, as long as λ<μ\lambda < \mu. The failure point is the queue itself: if λ≥μ\lambda \geq \mu it grows without bound until memory or timeouts intervene. Scaling options are a faster server (raise μ\mu), more servers (M/M/c, §4.10.4) or less demand (caching, load shedding).

M/M/1 results

ρ=λμW=1μ−λ=S1−ρWq=ρμ−λL=ρ1−ρLq=ρ21−ρ\rho = \frac{\lambda}{\mu} \qquad W = \frac{1}{\mu - \lambda} = \frac{S}{1 - \rho} \qquad W_q = \frac{\rho}{\mu - \lambda} \qquad L = \frac{\rho}{1 - \rho} \qquad L_q = \frac{\rho^2}{1 - \rho}

Symbol Meaning Units
λ\lambda Average arrival rate jobs/second
μ\mu Average service rate of the server jobs/second
S=1/μS = 1/\mu Average service time seconds
ρ\rho Utilization: fraction of time the server is busy (must be <1< 1) dimensionless
WW Average time in system (waiting + service), i.e. response time seconds
WqW_q Average time waiting in the queue before service starts seconds
LL Average number of jobs in the system jobs
LqL_q Average number of jobs waiting in the queue jobs

Derivation sketch. Because arrivals are memoryless, the number of jobs in the system behaves like a random walk that steps up at rate λ\lambda and down at rate μ\mu. Balancing the flow between neighboring states gives P(n jobs)=(1−ρ)ρnP(n \text{ jobs}) = (1 - \rho)\rho^n, a geometric distribution. Its mean is L=ρ/(1−ρ)L = \rho/(1-\rho). Little’s Law (§4.11) then gives W=L/λ=1/(μ−λ)W = L/\lambda = 1/(\mu - \lambda). A further useful fact: in M/M/1 the response time itself is exponentially distributed with rate μ−λ\mu - \lambda, so its qq-th percentile is W×ln11−qW \times \ln\frac{1}{1 - q}; the p99 is W×ln100=4.6WW \times \ln 100 = 4.6\,W [Harchol-Balter 2013].

Worked example — One server at increasing load. A service handles requests in 10 ms on average (μ=100\mu = 100/s).

  1. At λ=50\lambda = 50/s: ρ=0.5\rho = 0.5; W=1/(100−50)=0.020W = 1/(100 - 50) = 0.020 s = 20 ms; L=0.5/0.5=1L = 0.5/0.5 = 1 request.
  2. At λ=80\lambda = 80/s: ρ=0.8\rho = 0.8; W=1/20=50W = 1/20 = 50 ms; L=0.8/0.2=4L = 0.8/0.2 = 4.
  3. At λ=90\lambda = 90/s: ρ=0.9\rho = 0.9; W=1/10=100W = 1/10 = 100 ms; L=9L = 9; Lq=0.81/0.1=8.1L_q = 0.81/0.1 = 8.1; p99 =4.605×100≈461= 4.605 \times 100 \approx 461 ms.
  4. At λ=99\lambda = 99/s: ρ=0.99\rho = 0.99; W=1/1=1,000W = 1/1 = 1{,}000 ms.

Interpretation. Going from 50% to 90% utilization (1.8× the traffic) multiplies mean latency by 5, and the last 9% of traffic (90 → 99/s) multiplies it by another 10. Engineering implication. Plan latency-sensitive services to run at moderate utilization at peak — often 50–70% for interactive work — and reserve high utilization for batch work whose latency nobody waits for.

Table 4.5 — M/M/1 response time as a multiple of service time.

Utilization ρ\rho W/S=1/(1−ρ)W / S = 1/(1-\rho) WW when SS = 10 ms Jobs in system LL p99 when SS = 10 ms
0.50 2 20 ms 1 92 ms
0.70 3.3 33 ms 2.3 154 ms
0.80 5 50 ms 4 230 ms
0.90 10 100 ms 9 461 ms
0.95 20 200 ms 19 921 ms
0.99 100 1,000 ms 99 4,605 ms

4.10.3 Why latency explodes near 100% utilization

The factor 1/(1−ρ)1/(1 - \rho) is the whole story. The distance to saturation, 1−ρ1 - \rho, is in the denominator, so each halving of the remaining headroom doubles the latency: 0.8 → 0.9 doubles WW, 0.9 → 0.95 doubles it again, and so on. The curve is the familiar “hockey stick”. Two practical consequences follow:

  • Small traffic increases near saturation cause large latency increases. A service at 90% that sees a 5% traffic spike moves to 94.5%, and its mean latency nearly doubles.
  • Overload is not graceful. At ρ≥1\rho \geq 1 there is no steady state: the queue grows for as long as the overload lasts, and every request that joins it waits for all earlier ones. Bounded queues, timeouts and load shedding (§22.9) exist to convert unbounded latency into fast, explicit rejection.

The M/M/1 model assumes exponential service times. Real service times can be more or less variable; the general Pollaczek–Khinchine formula for the M/G/1 queue shows that mean queueing delay is proportional to (1+CS2)/2(1 + C_S^2)/2, where CSC_S is the coefficient of variation (standard deviation divided by mean) of the service time [Harchol-Balter 2013]. Exponential service has CS=1C_S = 1; perfectly constant service (CS=0C_S = 0) halves the queueing delay; heavy-tailed service (CS≫1C_S \gg 1) multiplies it. The 1/(1−ρ)1/(1-\rho) explosion is present in all of them.

The following simulation checks the M/M/1 formula. It uses the recurrence “a job starts when it arrives or when the previous job finishes, whichever is later”.

import random

def simulate_mm1(lam, mu, n_customers=200_000, seed=1):
    """Simulate a FIFO single-server queue with Poisson arrivals and
    exponential service times. Returns mean time in system (seconds)."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    arrival = 0.0          # arrival time of current customer
    server_free_at = 0.0   # time at which the server finishes its current job
    total_time = 0.0
    for _ in range(n_customers):
        arrival += rng.expovariate(lam)            # next arrival
        start = max(arrival, server_free_at)       # wait if server busy
        server_free_at = start + rng.expovariate(mu)
        total_time += server_free_at - arrival     # queueing + service
    return total_time / n_customers

mu = 100.0  # server completes 100 requests/s on average (10 ms each)
print(" rho   formula W (ms)   simulated W (ms)")
for lam in (50, 80, 90, 95, 99):
    formula = 1 / (mu - lam)
    sim = simulate_mm1(lam, mu)
    print(f"{lam/mu:4.2f}   {formula*1000:12.1f}   {sim*1000:14.1f}")

Output:

 rho   formula W (ms)   simulated W (ms)
0.50           20.0             20.0
0.80           50.0             49.7
0.90          100.0             98.6
0.95          200.0            220.4
0.99         1000.0           1059.1

What to notice:

  • At moderate utilization 200,000 simulated requests match the formula to within about 1%.
  • Near saturation the simulation is noisy (±6–10% here) even with 200,000 requests: the queue drifts through long busy periods, so averages converge slowly. Load tests near saturation need long runs for the same reason.
  • max(arrival, server_free_at) is the entire queueing mechanism: waiting happens only when a job arrives before the previous one finishes.

4.10.4 Multiple servers: M/M/c intuition

With cc identical servers sharing one queue (M/M/c), a job waits only if all cc servers are busy. The probability of waiting is given by the Erlang C formula; utilization is ρ=λ/(cμ)\rho = \lambda/(c\mu).

M/M/c (Erlang C)

a=λμ,ρ=ac,Pwait=acc!(1−ρ)∑k=0c−1akk!+acc!(1−ρ),W=Pwaitcμ−λ+1μa = \frac{\lambda}{\mu}, \quad \rho = \frac{a}{c}, \quad P_{\text{wait}} = \frac{\dfrac{a^c}{c!\,(1-\rho)}}{\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{c-1}\frac{a^k}{k!} + \frac{a^c}{c!\,(1-\rho)}}, \quad W = \frac{P_{\text{wait}}}{c\mu - \lambda} + \frac{1}{\mu}

Symbol Meaning Units
cc Number of servers sharing one queue count
μ\mu Service rate of each server jobs/second
aa Offered load: average number of busy servers servers (Erlangs)
ρ\rho Per-server utilization (<1<1) dimensionless
PwaitP_{\text{wait}} Probability an arriving job finds all servers busy dimensionless
WW Mean response time seconds

Figure 4.4 — One shared queue versus separate queues.

Reading the diagram. Both subgraphs have the same hardware (two servers at 50 jobs/s) and the same demand (80 jobs/s, ρ=0.8\rho = 0.8). On the left, any idle server takes the next job from a shared queue. On the right, each job is assigned to a server’s private queue at arrival, so one queue can hold waiting jobs while the other server sits idle. All paths are synchronous hand-offs. The failure point on the right is imbalance; the scaling lesson is that pooling beats partitioning for latency.

Worked example — Pooling. λ=80\lambda = 80/s; compare three designs with 100 jobs/s of total capacity.

  1. One fast server (M/M/1, μ=100\mu = 100): W=1/(100−80)=50W = 1/(100 - 80) = 50 ms.
  2. Two slow servers, separate queues (each M/M/1 with λ=40\lambda = 40, μ=50\mu = 50): W=1/(50−40)=100W = 1/(50-40) = 100 ms.
  3. Two slow servers, shared queue (M/M/2, μ=50\mu = 50): a=80/50=1.6a = 80/50 = 1.6, ρ=0.8\rho = 0.8. Numerator: a2/(2!(1−0.8))=2.56/0.4=6.4a^2/(2!\,(1-0.8)) = 2.56/0.4 = 6.4. Denominator: 1+1.6+6.4=91 + 1.6 + 6.4 = 9. Pwait=6.4/9=0.711P_{\text{wait}} = 6.4/9 = 0.711. W=0.711/(100−80)+1/50=0.0356+0.020=55.6W = 0.711/(100-80) + 1/50 = 0.0356 + 0.020 = 55.6 ms.

Interpretation. The shared queue (55.6 ms) is nearly as good as one server twice as fast (50 ms) and almost twice as good as separate queues (100 ms) on identical hardware. Engineering implication. Prefer a shared work queue (one listen socket feeding a pool of workers, one broker topic with competing consumers) over static assignment. Load-balancing algorithms such as least-connections and power-of-two-choices (§19.4) approximate a shared queue across machines.

import math

def erlang_c(c, lam, mu):
    """Probability that an arriving request must wait (M/M/c, Erlang C)."""
    a = lam / mu                 # offered load in "servers' worth" of work
    rho = a / c                  # per-server utilization
    if rho >= 1:
        return 1.0
    top = a**c / (math.factorial(c) * (1 - rho))
    bottom = sum(a**k / math.factorial(k) for k in range(c)) + top
    return top / bottom

def mmc_response_time(c, lam, mu):
    """Mean time in system W for an M/M/c queue (seconds)."""
    wait = erlang_c(c, lam, mu) / (c * mu - lam)
    return wait + 1 / mu

lam = 80.0
print(f"One fast server  (M/M/1, mu=100): W = {mmc_response_time(1, lam, 100)*1000:.1f} ms")
print(f"Two slow servers, shared queue (M/M/2, mu=50 each): "
      f"W = {mmc_response_time(2, lam, 50)*1000:.1f} ms")
print(f"Two slow servers, separate queues (2 x M/M/1, mu=50, lam=40 each): "
      f"W = {mmc_response_time(1, lam/2, 50)*1000:.1f} ms")

Output:

One fast server  (M/M/1, mu=100): W = 50.0 ms
Two slow servers, shared queue (M/M/2, mu=50 each): W = 55.6 ms
Two slow servers, separate queues (2 x M/M/1, mu=50, lam=40 each): W = 100.0 ms

What to notice: with c=1c = 1 the Erlang C function reduces to Pwait=ρP_{\text{wait}} = \rho and W=1/(μ−λ)W = 1/(\mu - \lambda), so the same code covers M/M/1. The rho >= 1 guard reflects that no steady state exists at or above saturation.

Mistake — “We are at 85% CPU, so we have 15% headroom.” Headroom in throughput is 15%, but latency at 85% is already 1/(1−0.85)=6.71/(1-0.85) = 6.7 times the service time in an M/M/1 model, and every further point of load costs more latency than the last. Express headroom as the latency you will have at the forecast peak, not as spare percentage.

4.11 Little’s Law

4.11.1 Statement and intuition

Definition — Little’s Law. For any stable system observed over a long period, the average number of items in the system equals the average arrival rate multiplied by the average time each item spends in the system: L=λWL = \lambda W [Little 1961].

First-principles explanation

A café serves 20 customers per hour, and each customer stays for 30 minutes on average. How many customers are inside at a typical moment? Every hour 20 people come in, each contributing half an hour of “presence”, so the café accumulates 20×0.5=1020 \times 0.5 = 10 customer-hours of presence per hour: on average 10 people are inside. That is all Little’s Law says. Remarkably, it does not depend on the arrival pattern, the service-time distribution, the number of servers or the scheduling order. It needs only that the system is stable (what goes in eventually comes out) and that the three quantities are long-run averages measured over the same boundary.

Little’s Law

L=λ×WL = \lambda \times W

Symbol Meaning Units
LL Average number of items in the system (concurrency, occupancy, in-flight requests) items
λ\lambda Average arrival rate (equals throughput in a stable system) items/second
WW Average time an item spends inside the system boundary seconds

Derivation intuition. Plot the number of items inside the system, N(t)N(t), over a long interval of length TT. The area under that curve can be computed two ways. Summed vertically, it is (average height) × (width) =L×T= L \times T. Summed horizontally, each item contributes a horizontal strip as long as its stay, so the area is (number of items) × (average stay) =λT×W= \lambda T \times W. Equating the two gives LT=λTWL T = \lambda T W, i.e. L=λWL = \lambda W. Little’s 1961 paper made this argument rigorous.

Because the law holds for any boundary, you can draw the boundary around a thread pool, a connection pool, a broker topic, a whole datacenter or a single CPU, and solve for whichever of the three quantities you do not know.

Figure 4.5 — Choosing the boundary for Little’s Law.

Reading the diagram. Clients send HTTPS requests to a load balancer, which forwards plain HTTP to a service instance. Inside the instance (boundary 1) each request occupies a worker thread for its whole duration, and briefly borrows a database connection to issue SQL to PostgreSQL (boundary 2, the storage boundary). All calls are synchronous. Little’s Law applies separately to each boundary: threads in use = request rate × request duration; connections in use = query rate × connection hold time. The failure point is any pool whose occupancy LL approaches its size, because requests then queue for a thread or connection. Scaling options are more instances (spreading λ\lambda), shorter hold times (reducing WW) or larger pools (raising the limit on LL).

4.11.2 Capacity planning examples

Worked example 1 — Sizing a thread pool. A service receives 2,000 RPS at peak, spread across 8 instances. Each request holds a worker thread for 80 ms on average (mostly waiting on downstream calls).

  1. Per-instance arrival rate: λ=2,000/8=250\lambda = 2{,}000 / 8 = 250 RPS.
  2. Average busy threads: L=λW=250×0.080=20L = \lambda W = 250 \times 0.080 = 20 threads.
  3. A pool of exactly 20 would run at 100% utilization and queue without bound (§4.10). Treat the pool as an M/M/c system with cc threads, μ=1/0.08=12.5\mu = 1/0.08 = 12.5/s per thread and a=20a = 20.
  4. Using the Erlang C code of §4.10.4: with c=25c = 25 (ρ=0.80\rho = 0.80), 20.9% of requests wait for a thread and mean latency is 83.4 ms; with c=30c = 30 (ρ=0.67\rho = 0.67), 2.5% wait and latency is 80.2 ms; with c=35c = 35, 0.16% wait.

Interpretation. Little’s Law gives the average concurrency (20); queueing theory tells you how much headroom above it buys acceptable waiting. Engineering implication. Size the pool around 30 threads per instance, and re-derive it whenever WW changes: if a downstream dependency slows from 80 ms to 400 ms, required concurrency jumps to 250×0.4=100250 \times 0.4 = 100 threads, and a 30-thread pool saturates. That is why per-dependency timeouts and bulkheads (§22.11, §22.14) are capacity mechanisms, not just error handling.

Worked example 2 — Sizing a database connection pool. 30 application instances together issue 1,200 queries per second. Each query holds a connection for 5 ms (network round trip plus execution).

  1. Connections in use, fleet-wide: L=1,200×0.005=6L = 1{,}200 \times 0.005 = 6 connections on average.
  2. Per instance: λ=1,200/30=40\lambda = 1{,}200/30 = 40 queries/s, so L=40×0.005=0.2L = 40 \times 0.005 = 0.2 connections.
  3. A common default of 10 connections per instance opens 30×10=30030 \times 10 = 300 connections to serve an average demand of 6.
  4. Incident case: a missing index makes queries take 500 ms. Now L=1,200×0.5=600L = 1{,}200 \times 0.5 = 600 connections are needed — more than the 300 that exist, so requests queue for connections, threads block, and the outage spreads upstream.

Interpretation. The pool is 50× oversized in normal operation and still too small during the incident. Engineering implication. Oversized pools are not free: in PostgreSQL each connection is a separate server process with its own memory, so hundreds of mostly idle connections waste database resources and let a slow-query incident push far more concurrent work onto an already struggling database. A small pool (here perhaps 2–3 per instance) or a central pooler such as PgBouncer (§14.13), combined with query timeouts, caps concurrency at the database where it matters.

Worked example 3 — Inferring latency from a backlog. A message broker topic holds a backlog of 5,000 messages, and consumers process 1,000 messages per second while producers add messages at the same rate.

  1. Rearranging Little’s Law: W=L/λ=5,000/1,000=5W = L / \lambda = 5{,}000 / 1{,}000 = 5 s.

Interpretation. Each message spends about 5 s waiting in the topic before processing. Engineering implication. Consumer lag measured in messages (the metric most brokers expose) converts to lag in seconds — the metric users care about — by dividing by throughput. Alert on the latter.

Mistake — Mixing boundaries. Little’s Law requires that LL, λ\lambda and WW are measured on the same boundary. Using end-to-end request latency (which includes time spent in the database) with the occupancy of the application thread pool is correct only if threads are held for the entire request. If an asynchronous framework releases the thread while waiting for I/O, the thread-holding time WW is much smaller than request latency.

4.12 Amdahl’s Law and Gustafson’s Law

4.12.1 Amdahl’s Law

Definition — Speedup. The ratio of the time a job takes on one processor (or node) to the time it takes on NN: S(N)=T(1)/T(N)S(N) = T(1)/T(N). Perfect, linear speedup is S(N)=NS(N) = N.

First-principles explanation

Eight friends cook a dinner. Chopping vegetables parallelizes beautifully: eight people chop eight times faster. But the oven takes 40 minutes no matter how many cooks there are. However many friends you add, dinner cannot take less than 40 minutes. Gene Amdahl made this argument in 1967 about parallel computers [Amdahl 1967]: the part of a job that cannot be parallelized sets a hard ceiling on speedup.

Amdahl’s Law (fixed problem size)

S(N)=1(1−p)+pNlimN→∞S(N)=11−pS(N) = \frac{1}{(1 - p) + \dfrac{p}{N}} \qquad \lim_{N \to \infty} S(N) = \frac{1}{1 - p}

Symbol Meaning Units
pp Fraction of the single-processor run time that can be parallelized dimensionless (0–1)
1−p1 - p Serial fraction dimensionless
NN Number of processors, cores or nodes count
S(N)S(N) Speedup relative to one processor dimensionless (×)

Derivation. Normalize the one-processor time to 1. The serial part still takes 1−p1 - p; the parallel part takes p/Np/N on NN processors. Speedup is the old time (1) divided by the new time.

Worked example — A 95% parallel job. A batch job spends 5% of its time in a single-threaded setup phase and 95% in work that splits perfectly across cores.

  1. On 8 cores: S=1/(0.05+0.95/8)=1/(0.05+0.11875)=1/0.16875=5.93S = 1/(0.05 + 0.95/8) = 1/(0.05 + 0.11875) = 1/0.16875 = 5.93.
  2. On 64 cores: S=1/(0.05+0.01484)=1/0.06484=15.4S = 1/(0.05 + 0.01484) = 1/0.06484 = 15.4.
  3. Ceiling: 1/0.05=201/0.05 = 20, however many cores.
  4. Efficiency on 64 cores: 15.4/64=24%15.4/64 = 24\%.

Interpretation. Moving from 8 to 64 cores (8× the hardware) improves speed only 2.6×. Engineering implication. Before buying more parallelism, measure and shrink the serial fraction: a single-threaded coordinator, a global lock, a sequential merge step. Cutting the serial fraction from 5% to 1% raises the ceiling from 20 to 100.

4.12.2 Gustafson’s Law

Amdahl assumes a fixed problem. In practice, when engineers get more machines they usually tackle bigger problems — more data, higher resolution, larger models — in the same wall-clock time. John Gustafson observed in 1988 that under this assumption the serial part stays roughly constant while the parallel part grows with NN [Gustafson 1988].

Gustafson’s Law (scaled problem size)

Sscaled(N)=(1−p)+pN=N−(1−p)(N−1)S_{\text{scaled}}(N) = (1 - p) + p\,N = N - (1 - p)(N - 1)

Symbol Meaning Units
pp Fraction of the parallel run’s time spent in parallel work dimensionless
1−p1 - p Fraction of the parallel run’s time that is serial dimensionless
NN Number of processors count
SscaledS_{\text{scaled}} How much more work is completed in the same time than one processor could do dimensionless (×)

Worked example — The same 5% serial fraction, scaled. On 64 processors a job spends 5% of its wall-clock time in serial work.

  1. Sscaled=0.05+0.95×64=0.05+60.8=60.85S_{\text{scaled}} = 0.05 + 0.95 \times 64 = 0.05 + 60.8 = 60.85.

Interpretation. 64 processors complete about 61 times as much work as one would in the same time, versus Amdahl’s 15.4 for a fixed problem. The laws do not contradict each other; they answer different questions (“how much faster?” vs “how much bigger?”). Engineering implication. Horizontal scaling of data-parallel systems (MapReduce, Spark, distributed training) mostly lives in Gustafson’s world: more nodes handle more data. Latency-sensitive single requests live in Amdahl’s world: more nodes do not make one request much faster.

4.13 The Universal Scalability Law

4.13.1 Beyond Amdahl: coordination costs

Amdahl’s Law predicts that adding nodes never hurts: throughput keeps rising toward a ceiling. Real systems often get slower past some size. Neil Gunther’s Universal Scalability Law (USL) explains why by adding a second penalty: coherency (or crosstalk), the cost of nodes keeping each other consistent [Gunther 2007].

First-principles explanation

Return to the kitchen. Contention is the queue for the single oven (Amdahl’s serial part). Coherency is the time cooks spend talking to each other — “did you already salt this?”. If every cook must check with every other cook, the number of conversations grows like N(N−1)N(N-1), roughly N2N^2. With few cooks this is negligible; with many it dominates, and adding a cook makes dinner later.

Universal Scalability Law

C(N)=N1+α(N−1)+βN(N−1)N*=1−αβC(N) = \frac{N}{1 + \alpha(N - 1) + \beta N (N - 1)} \qquad N^{*} = \sqrt{\frac{1 - \alpha}{\beta}}

Symbol Meaning Units
NN Number of nodes, cores, threads or concurrent users count
C(N)C(N) Relative capacity: throughput at NN divided by throughput at 1 dimensionless (×)
α\alpha Contention coefficient: serialization on shared resources (queues, locks) dimensionless (0–1)
β\beta Coherency coefficient: pairwise coordination cost (cache coherence, consensus, data exchange) dimensionless (≥ 0)
N*N^{*} Concurrency at which throughput peaks count

Gunther’s later work writes the coefficients as σ\sigma (contention) and κ\kappa (coherency); the formula is the same. With β=0\beta = 0 the USL reduces exactly to Amdahl’s Law with serial fraction α\alpha. N*N^* comes from setting the derivative of C(N)C(N) to zero.

Worked example — Where adding nodes stops helping. A clustered service is measured and fitted with α=0.05\alpha = 0.05 and β=0.001\beta = 0.001.

  1. C(8)=8/(1+0.05×7+0.001×8×7)=8/(1+0.35+0.056)=8/1.406=5.69C(8) = 8 / (1 + 0.05 \times 7 + 0.001 \times 8 \times 7) = 8 / (1 + 0.35 + 0.056) = 8/1.406 = 5.69.
  2. C(32)=32/(1+1.55+0.992)=32/3.542=9.03C(32) = 32 / (1 + 1.55 + 0.992) = 32/3.542 = 9.03.
  3. C(64)=64/(1+3.15+4.032)=64/8.182=7.82C(64) = 64 / (1 + 3.15 + 4.032) = 64/8.182 = 7.82.
  4. Peak: N*=(1−0.05)/0.001=950=30.8N^* = \sqrt{(1 - 0.05)/0.001} = \sqrt{950} = 30.8 nodes.

Interpretation. Throughput peaks around 31 nodes at about 9× a single node; doubling to 64 nodes loses 13% of throughput. Amdahl with the same α\alpha predicts 15.4× at 64 nodes. Engineering implication. If load tests show throughput flattening and then falling as you add nodes or threads, look for coherency costs: all-to-all communication, cache-line ping-pong, distributed locks, broadcast invalidation. The cure is architectural (partitioning so that nodes rarely coordinate), not more hardware.

import math

def amdahl(p, n):
    """Speedup with n processors when fraction p of the work is parallel."""
    return 1 / ((1 - p) + p / n)

def gustafson(p, n):
    """Scaled speedup when the parallel part grows with n."""
    return (1 - p) + p * n

def usl(n, alpha, beta):
    """Relative capacity C(n) under the Universal Scalability Law."""
    return n / (1 + alpha * (n - 1) + beta * n * (n - 1))

p, alpha, beta = 0.95, 0.05, 0.001
print("   N  Amdahl  Gustafson   USL")
for n in (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128):
    print(f"{n:4d}  {amdahl(p, n):6.2f}  {gustafson(p, n):9.2f}  {usl(n, alpha, beta):5.2f}")
n_star = math.sqrt((1 - alpha) / beta)
print(f"USL peak at N* = {n_star:.1f}; Amdahl ceiling = {1/(1-p):.0f}")

Table 4.6 — Output: three scaling models with a 5% serial fraction.

N Amdahl Gustafson USL (α\alpha=0.05, β\beta=0.001)
1 1.00 1.00 1.00
2 1.90 1.95 1.90
4 3.48 3.85 3.44
8 5.93 7.65 5.69
16 9.14 15.25 8.04
32 12.55 30.45 9.03
64 15.42 60.85 7.82
128 17.41 121.65 5.42

The program also prints USL peak at N* = 30.8; Amdahl ceiling = 20. What to notice: the three columns agree for small NN, which is why a few measurements at low concurrency cannot distinguish the models. Measure out to the concurrency you intend to run. In practice the USL coefficients are fitted by regression to throughput measured at several values of NN [Gunther 2007]; Chapter 23 (§23.10) shows the workflow.

Mistake — Extrapolating linear scaling from a small test. “Two nodes gave 1.9×, so 100 nodes will give 95×.” Every model in Table 4.6 is nearly linear at N=2N = 2. Contention and coherency only show up at scale, so linear extrapolation is the most common way capacity plans fail.

4.14 Availability arithmetic

4.14.1 Nines and downtime budgets

Definition — Availability. The fraction of time (or of requests) for which a system serves correctly: A=uptime/(uptime+downtime)A = \text{uptime}/(\text{uptime} + \text{downtime}), or, request-based, A=successful requests/valid requestsA = \text{successful requests} / \text{valid requests}. It is commonly quoted in “nines”: 99.9% is “three nines”.

Table 4.7 — Nines and the downtime they allow (365-day year, 30-day month, 7-day week).

Availability Nines Downtime per year Downtime per month Downtime per week
90% 1 36.5 days 72 h 16.8 h
99% 2 3.65 days (87.6 h) 7.2 h 1.68 h
99.9% 3 8.76 h 43.2 min 10.1 min
99.95% 3.5 4.38 h 21.6 min 5.04 min
99.99% 4 52.6 min 4.32 min 60.5 s
99.999% 5 5.26 min 25.9 s 6.05 s
99.9999% 6 31.5 s 2.59 s 0.60 s

Downtime budget

D=(1−A)×TD = (1 - A) \times T

Symbol Meaning Units
AA Availability target dimensionless
TT Length of the period minutes (or any time unit)
DD Allowed downtime in the period (the error budget, in time) same unit as TT

Worked example — What four nines allows. Target A=99.99%A = 99.99\% over a 30-day month.

  1. T=30×24×60=43,200T = 30 \times 24 \times 60 = 43{,}200 min.
  2. D=0.0001×43,200=4.32D = 0.0001 \times 43{,}200 = 4.32 min.

Interpretation. Four minutes and 19 seconds per month, total. Engineering implication. A human cannot be paged, wake up, log in and diagnose in four minutes. Four nines therefore implies automated detection and failover; five nines (26 s/month) implies the failover itself must be nearly invisible. Each additional nine changes the architecture, not just the effort.

Google SRE — error budgets. Google’s SRE practice turns an availability SLO into an error budget equal to 1−SLO1 - \text{SLO}: a 99.9% SLO allows 0.1% of requests (or time) to fail. While budget remains, teams may ship risky changes; when it is exhausted, releases slow until reliability recovers. The SRE book also argues that 100% is the wrong target, because users cannot distinguish the last nines from failures in their own devices and networks, while each extra nine costs disproportionately more. Error budgets are covered in §39.7. Evidence: Primary — [Beyer et al. 2016]

4.14.2 Series and parallel composition

Figure 4.6 — Series, parallel and k-of-n availability.

Reading the diagram. A request flows synchronously left to right: HTTPS from the client to a single load balancer, then to either application node, then over SQL to the current leader replica (Replica 1), which replicates each write to the other two and needs a majority (2 of 3) of replicas up to serve, as consensus-based stores do (§26.4); if the leader fails, a surviving replica is elected in its place. The three stages are in series: the request fails if any stage fails. Within the middle stage the two nodes are in parallel: the stage fails only if both fail. The cylinders are the storage boundary. The single load balancer is the obvious single point of failure; the scaling and availability option is to make it redundant too (§19.8).

Series, parallel and k-of-n availability (independent failures)

Aseries=∏i=1nAiAparallel=1−∏i=1n(1−Ai)Ak-of-n=∑j=kn(nj)Aj(1−A)n−jA_{\text{series}} = \prod_{i=1}^{n} A_i \qquad A_{\text{parallel}} = 1 - \prod_{i=1}^{n} (1 - A_i) \qquad A_{k\text{-of-}n} = \sum_{j=k}^{n} \binom{n}{j} A^j (1 - A)^{n-j}

Symbol Meaning Units
AiA_i Availability of component ii dimensionless
∏\prod Product over all components —
nn Number of components count
kk Minimum number of identical components that must be up count
AA Availability of each identical component (k-of-n case) dimensionless

Derivation. Series: the system is up only if every component is up; with independence, multiply. Parallel: the system is down only if every component is down; the probability all are down is ∏(1−Ai)\prod(1 - A_i), and availability is its complement. k-of-n: the number of up components is binomial (§4.6.4); add the probabilities of k,k+1,…,nk, k+1, \ldots, n components up.

Worked example — Composing the system of Figure 4.6.

  1. Series of three single components first, for intuition: LB 99.99%, one app node 99.95%, one database 99.9%: 0.9999×0.9995×0.999=0.998400.9999 \times 0.9995 \times 0.999 = 0.99840, i.e. 99.84%, about 14.0 h of downtime per year — worse than the weakest component.
  2. Parallel app tier: two nodes at 99%: 1−(0.01)2=1−0.0001=0.99991 - (0.01)^2 = 1 - 0.0001 = 0.9999.
  3. 2-of-3 database: A=0.99A = 0.99: (32)(0.99)2(0.01)+(0.99)3=3×0.9801×0.01+0.970299=0.029403+0.970299=0.999702\binom{3}{2}(0.99)^2(0.01) + (0.99)^3 = 3 \times 0.9801 \times 0.01 + 0.970299 = 0.029403 + 0.970299 = 0.999702.
  4. Whole system in series: 0.9999×0.9999×0.999702=0.9995020.9999 \times 0.9999 \times 0.999702 = 0.999502, about 4.4 h of downtime per year.

Interpretation. Series composition always lowers availability; redundancy raises it dramatically — two 99% nodes give 99.99%. Engineering implication. A request path through 10 services, each 99.9% available, is at most 0.99910=99.0%0.999^{10} = 99.0\% available. Long synchronous call chains are an availability liability, which is one argument for asynchronous decoupling (Part VI) and for keeping critical paths short.

from math import comb, prod

def series(*avail):
    """All components must be up (assumes independent failures)."""
    return prod(avail)

def parallel(*avail):
    """At least one component must be up (independent failures)."""
    return 1 - prod(1 - a for a in avail)

def k_of_n(k, n, a):
    """At least k of n identical, independent components must be up."""
    return sum(comb(n, i) * a**i * (1 - a)**(n - i) for i in range(k, n + 1))

def downtime_per_year(a, hours_per_year=365 * 24):
    return (1 - a) * hours_per_year

web_tier = parallel(0.99, 0.99)          # two app nodes behind a load balancer
db_quorum = k_of_n(2, 3, 0.99)           # 2-of-3 replicated database
system = series(0.9999, web_tier, db_quorum)   # LB -> web tier -> DB

for name, a in [("web tier", web_tier), ("db 2-of-3", db_quorum), ("system", system)]:
    print(f"{name:10s} A = {a:.6f}  downtime = {downtime_per_year(a):6.2f} h/year")

Output:

web tier   A = 0.999900  downtime =   0.88 h/year
db 2-of-3  A = 0.999702  downtime =   2.61 h/year
system     A = 0.999502  downtime =   4.36 h/year

What to notice: series, parallel and k_of_n compose — the result of one can be fed into another to model any tree of components. Every function assumes independent failures, so the outputs are upper bounds on what a real system with shared dependencies achieves.

Warning — Redundancy arithmetic is only as good as its independence assumption. Two app nodes deployed by the same bad configuration push fail together; three replicas on one power feed fail together. Also, parallel redundancy requires failover to work: if detecting a failure and rerouting takes 30 s, each failure still costs 30 s of errors. Model failover time explicitly, and place replicas in separate failure domains (racks, zones, regions; §39.4).

4.15 Reliability: MTBF, MTTR and failure rates

4.15.1 Definitions

Definition — Reliability, MTBF, MTTR and failure rate. Reliability R(t)R(t) is the probability that a component operates without failure for a period of length tt. The mean time between failures (MTBF) is the average operating time from the end of one repair to the next failure (for non-repairable parts the same quantity is called MTTF, mean time to failure). The mean time to repair (MTTR) is the average time from failure to restored service, including detection, diagnosis and repair. The failure rate λ\lambda is the average number of failures per unit of operating time.

First-principles explanation

Availability asks “what fraction of the time is it working?”. Reliability asks “how likely is it to keep working for the next hour (or day, or job)?”. A car that breaks down every week but is fixed in five minutes by the roadside is highly available and poorly reliable; a car that never breaks down for a year but then spends a month in the garage is the opposite. Both properties matter, for different users (§4.18.2).

Reliability and availability from MTBF and MTTR

λ=1MTBFR(t)=e−λtA=MTBFMTBF+MTTRAFR=1−e−8760/MTTF\lambda = \frac{1}{\text{MTBF}} \qquad R(t) = e^{-\lambda t} \qquad A = \frac{\text{MTBF}}{\text{MTBF} + \text{MTTR}} \qquad \text{AFR} = 1 - e^{-8760/\text{MTTF}}

Symbol Meaning Units
MTBF Mean operating time between failures hours
MTTR Mean time to repair (detect + diagnose + fix + restore) hours
MTTF Mean time to failure of a non-repairable part hours
λ\lambda Constant failure rate failures/hour
