              "exp": now + ttl_s, "jti": str(uuid.uuid4()), "scope": " ".join(scopes)}
    return jwt.encode(claims, private_key, algorithm="RS256",
                      headers={"kid": "2026-10-key-1"})

# Resource server: holds only the public key.
def validate_access_token(token: str) -> dict:
    return jwt.decode(
        token, public_pem,
        algorithms=["RS256"],               # pin the algorithm; never trust the header
        audience=AUDIENCE, issuer=ISSUER,
        leeway=30,                          # tolerate 30 s of clock skew
        options={"require": ["exp", "iat", "sub", "aud", "iss"]},
    )

token = issue_access_token("user-123", ["articles:read", "articles:write"])
print(len(token), validate_access_token(token)["scope"])   # ~700 articles:read articles:write

What to notice:

  • algorithms=["RS256"] defends against two classic attacks: tokens with "alg": "none" (no signature at all), and algorithm confusion, where an attacker signs an HS256 token using the server’s public RSA key as the HMAC secret and a careless library verifies it [RFC 8725].
  • The token is about 700 characters; at 10,000 requests per second that is about 7 MB/s of header bytes, which HTTP/2 header compression reduces on reused connections.
  • In a FastAPI service, the same validation sits in a dependency that returns 401 or 403 with RFC 6750 WWW-Authenticate errors:
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, HTTPException
from fastapi.security import HTTPAuthorizationCredentials, HTTPBearer

app = FastAPI()
bearer = HTTPBearer(auto_error=False)

def current_claims(creds: HTTPAuthorizationCredentials | None = Depends(bearer)) -> dict:
    if creds is None:
        raise HTTPException(401, "Missing bearer token",
                            headers={"WWW-Authenticate": 'Bearer realm="api"'})
    try:
        return validate_access_token(creds.credentials)
    except jwt.InvalidTokenError:
        raise HTTPException(401, "Invalid or expired token",
                            headers={"WWW-Authenticate": 'Bearer error="invalid_token"'})

def require_scope(scope: str):
    def checker(claims: dict = Depends(current_claims)) -> dict:
        if scope not in claims.get("scope", "").split():
            raise HTTPException(403, f"Requires scope {scope}", headers={
                "WWW-Authenticate": f'Bearer error="insufficient_scope", scope="{scope}"'})
        return claims
    return checker

@app.delete("/v1/articles/{article_id}", status_code=204)
def delete_article(article_id: int, claims: dict = Depends(require_scope("articles:delete"))):
    ...   # delete, recording claims["sub"] in the audit log

8.13.4 The revocation problem

Because verification is local, a server cannot know that a token was revoked — after logout, a password change, or a stolen laptop — until it expires. Mitigations, usually combined:

  1. Short access-token lifetimes (5–15 minutes) plus refresh tokens (§8.14.4), which are checked against a server-side store on each refresh.
  2. Deny-list by jti (or by sub + “tokens issued before time T”) in a fast replicated store, checked on each request. This reintroduces a lookup, but the list holds only revoked, not-yet-expired tokens.
  3. Token introspection (RFC 7662): the resource server asks the authorization server whether a token is active, which trades the local-verification advantage for immediacy; often used only for high-risk operations.

Worked example — Revocation window and deny-list size. Access tokens live T=15T = 15 min. Users revoke sessions at r=100r = 100 per minute.

  1. Worst-case exposure after revocation without a deny-list: up to 15 min; if revocation times are uniformly distributed relative to issuance, on average 7.5 min.
  2. Deny-list size: entries need be kept only until the token would have expired anyway, so N=r×T=100×15=1,500N = r \times T = 100 \times 15 = 1{,}500 entries — about 1,500 × ~50 bytes ≈ 75 KB.

Interpretation. A deny-list is tiny and can be replicated into every service’s memory and refreshed every few seconds. Engineering implication: “JWTs cannot be revoked” is false; the cost is a small, bounded amount of shared state.

Storing JWTs in localStorage because “cookies are old-fashioned”. Any XSS bug can read localStorage and exfiltrate the token. For browser apps, an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite session cookie to your own backend (which holds the tokens server-side, the BFF pattern) is usually safer.

8.14 OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect

8.14.1 The delegation problem

Definition — OAuth 2.0. An authorization framework that lets a third-party application obtain limited access to an HTTP service on behalf of a resource owner, by obtaining an access token from an authorization server instead of using the owner’s credentials [RFC 6749].

Many cars come with a valet key: it starts the engine but cannot open the boot or the glovebox. You hand the valet a limited key instead of your full key ring. Before OAuth, a photo-printing site that wanted your photos from another service asked for your password — your full key ring — and could then do anything, forever, until you changed it. OAuth gives the printing site a valet key: a token scoped to “read photos”, time-limited, revocable, and issued without the site ever seeing your password.

8.14.2 Roles and grants

OAuth defines four roles [RFC 6749 §1.1]:

  • Resource owner — the user who owns the data.
  • Client — the application requesting access (the photo printer). A confidential client (a server-side app) can keep a client secret; a public client (SPA, mobile app) cannot, because its code is in users’ hands.
  • Authorization server (AS) — authenticates the owner, asks for consent and issues tokens.
  • Resource server (RS) — the API that accepts access tokens.

Tokens are presented as bearer tokens — “whoever bears this token may use it” — in the Authorization: Bearer <token> header, so they must only travel over TLS [RFC 6750].

Table 8.19 — OAuth 2.0 grant types and their status.

Grant Who uses it Status (as of 2026)
Authorization code + PKCE Web apps, SPAs, mobile and desktop apps acting for a user Recommended for all user-facing clients
Client credentials A service acting for itself (machine-to-machine) Recommended
Refresh token Any client renewing an access token Recommended, with rotation for public clients
Device authorization (RFC 8628) TVs and CLIs without a convenient browser Recommended for those devices
Implicit Old SPAs (token returned in the URL fragment) Deprecated; omitted from OAuth 2.1
Resource owner password credentials Client collects the user’s password Deprecated; omitted from OAuth 2.1

8.14.3 Authorization code flow with PKCE

Definition — PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange, “pixy”). An extension in which the client creates a random secret, the code verifier, sends only its SHA-256 hash, the code challenge, with the authorization request, and must present the verifier when redeeming the authorization code. An attacker who intercepts the code cannot redeem it without the verifier [RFC 7636].

Figure 8.11 — OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow with PKCE.

Reading the diagram. Steps 3–6 happen through the user’s browser via redirects (the front channel), where URLs can leak through history, logs and malicious apps registered for the same redirect scheme on mobile devices. The authorization server only ever sees the hash of the verifier there. Step 8 is a direct HTTPS call from client to authorization server (the back channel), where the client proves possession of the verifier; an attacker who stole the code in step 6 lacks it. The state value checked in step 7 stops an attacker from injecting their own authorization response into the user’s session (CSRF against the redirect endpoint). Steps 11–13 are ordinary API calls with a bearer token, validated as in §8.13.3 or by introspection. All calls are synchronous. Storage boundaries: the authorization server stores codes (single use, short-lived, typically under a minute), challenges, grants and refresh tokens. Failure points: the authorization server is on the login path for every user and must be highly available; resource servers that validate JWTs locally keep working during a brief AS outage until tokens expire. Scaling: token validation scales with the number of resource servers; the token endpoint scales like any stateless service backed by a replicated store.

import base64, hashlib, secrets

def make_pkce_pair() -> tuple[str, str]:
    # 32 random bytes -> 43-character base64url verifier (RFC 7636 allows 43-128 chars)
    verifier = base64.urlsafe_b64encode(secrets.token_bytes(32)).rstrip(b"=").decode()
    return verifier, challenge_for(verifier)

def challenge_for(verifier: str) -> str:
    digest = hashlib.sha256(verifier.encode("ascii")).digest()
    return base64.urlsafe_b64encode(digest).rstrip(b"=").decode()

# Test vector from RFC 7636 Appendix B:
assert challenge_for("dBjftJeZ4CVP-mB92K27uhbUJU1p1r_wW1gFWFOEjXk") == \
    "E9Melhoa2OwvFrEMTJguCHaoeK1t8URWbuGJSstw-cM"

The token exchange (step 8) on the wire:

curl -s https://auth.example.com/oauth/token \
  -d grant_type=authorization_code \
  -d code=SplxlOBeZQQYbYS6WxSbIA \
  -d redirect_uri=https://app.example.com/callback \
  -d client_id=photo-printer \
  -d code_verifier=dBjftJeZ4CVP-mB92K27uhbUJU1p1r_wW1gFWFOEjXk
# {"access_token":"eyJhbGciOi...","token_type":"Bearer","expires_in":900,
#  "refresh_token":"8xLOxBtZp8...","scope":"photos.read"}

What to notice: PKCE was designed for public clients, which have no secret; current guidance recommends it for confidential clients too [RFC 9700]. Redirect URIs must be registered in advance and matched exactly, since a loose match lets an attacker redirect codes to their own site.

8.14.4 Client credentials and refresh tokens

Client credentials grant. No user is involved: a backend service authenticates as itself (client ID plus secret, a signed JWT assertion, or mutual TLS) and receives a token scoped to the APIs it may call. This is the standard pattern for machine-to-machine calls between organizations or between internal services when not using mTLS identities (§10.10).

curl -s -u billing-service:$CLIENT_SECRET https://auth.example.com/oauth/token \
  -d grant_type=client_credentials -d scope=invoices.write

Refresh tokens let a client obtain new short-lived access tokens without user interaction. Because the refresh token is long-lived and is checked by the authorization server on each use, it is where revocation actually happens: revoke the refresh token and the client loses access within one access-token lifetime. For public clients, refresh-token rotation issues a new refresh token on every use and invalidates the old one; if an old one is ever presented again, the server assumes theft and revokes the whole token family [RFC 9700].

8.14.5 OAuth 2.1

OAuth 2.1 is an IETF Internet-Draft that consolidates RFC 6749, RFC 6750, PKCE and the security best current practice into one document: PKCE required for the authorization code grant, implicit and password grants removed, exact redirect-URI matching, and no bearer tokens in query strings. As of October 2026 it is still a draft (revision -16, September 2026), not an RFC [OAuth 2.1 draft]; in practice, following RFC 9700 gets you the same behavior today.

8.14.6 OpenID Connect

OAuth answers “may this app access these photos?” It deliberately says nothing about who the user is; an access token is meant for the resource server and may be opaque to the client. Applications nonetheless abused OAuth for “Sign in with …”, which caused vulnerabilities. OpenID Connect (OIDC) is a thin identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0 that standardizes login [OpenID Connect Core 1.0]:

  • The client requests scope=openid (plus profile, email as needed).
  • The token response additionally contains an ID token: a JWT for the client (its aud is the client ID) asserting who logged in — iss, sub (stable user identifier at that issuer), aud, exp, iat, auth_time, and the nonce the client sent, which prevents replay of an ID token into a different login.
  • A UserInfo endpoint returns profile claims for the access token.
  • Discovery (/.well-known/openid-configuration) publishes the issuer’s endpoints and its JWKS URL, so clients configure themselves from one URL.

Sending the ID token to your API as an access token, or accepting any provider’s access token as proof of login. The ID token’s audience is the client; the access token’s audience is the API. Validate each only for its intended audience. Identify users by the pair (iss, sub), never by email address alone, which can change or be reassigned.

8.15 API versioning and compatibility

8.15.1 What breaks clients

An API is a promise to every client that ever integrated with it. You cannot redeploy those clients; you can only stop breaking them. Applying the rules of §8.9.3 to HTTP APIs:

Table 8.20 — Breaking and non-breaking API changes.

Non-breaking (additive) Breaking
Add a new endpoint Remove or rename an endpoint or field
Add an optional request parameter Add a required request parameter
Add a field to a response Change a field’s type, format or meaning
Add a new enum value if clients were told to tolerate unknown values Add an enum value clients switch on exhaustively
Relax a validation rule Tighten validation; change defaults; change error codes
Add a new error type within an existing status Change pagination or authentication scheme

Clients share responsibility: a tolerant reader ignores unknown fields and unknown enum values instead of failing. Document that obligation explicitly.

8.15.2 Versioning strategies

Table 8.21 — API versioning strategies.

Strategy Example Advantages Disadvantages
URI path GET /v2/orders/42 Obvious; easy to route, cache and test in a browser A version is a whole parallel API; encourages big-bang versions
Custom header Api-Version: 2 Clean URIs Invisible in logs and links; caches must Vary on the header
Media type Accept: application/vnd.example.v2+json Most aligned with HTTP content negotiation Awkward tooling; rarely understood by clients
Date-based, pinned per client Stripe-Version: 2024-06-20 Small, frequent changes; each client upgrades on its own schedule Server must maintain transformations for every live version

Two practices that work regardless of the mechanism: use major versions only for breaking changes (additive changes need no new version), and keep the number of live major versions small (one or two).

Stripe’s date-based versions. Stripe pins each account to the API version current when it first made a request, and lets requests override it with a Stripe-Version header. Internally the latest code produces the latest response shape, and a chain of small “version change” modules transforms responses backwards, one step per version, to whatever version the client is pinned to. This lets Stripe ship breaking improvements frequently without forcing integrations to change [Leach 2017]. GitHub’s REST API similarly uses date-named versions selected by the X-GitHub-Api-Version header [GitHub Docs: API versions]. Evidence: Primary — [Leach 2017]; [GitHub Docs: API versions]

8.15.3 Deprecation

Deprecation is a process, not an event:

  1. Announce in the changelog and documentation, with a date.
  2. Signal in-band. Send the Deprecation response header [RFC 9745] on deprecated endpoints, a Link with rel="deprecation" pointing to migration docs, and the Sunset header [RFC 8594] with the date the endpoint will stop working.
  3. Measure. Log usage of deprecated endpoints per client ID; contact the remaining heavy users directly.
  4. Brown-outs. Before the sunset date, fail a small, increasing fraction of calls for short scheduled windows, so forgotten integrations surface while there is time to fix them.
  5. Remove, returning 410 Gone with a problem-details body that links to the migration guide.

Figure 8.12 — Lifecycle of an API version.

Reading the diagram. A version starts as a preview (no compatibility promise), becomes stable when its contract is frozen, and is deprecated once a successor is generally available; from then on responses carry Deprecation and Sunset headers. At the sunset date it is removed and answers 410 Gone. The transitions are driven by policy and calendar, not by traffic. Failure point: removing a version that still carries significant traffic; usage metrics per client must gate the final transition.

8.16 API documentation: OpenAPI

Definition — OpenAPI Specification (OAS). A vendor-neutral, machine-readable format (YAML or JSON) for describing HTTP APIs: paths, operations, parameters, request and response bodies (as JSON Schema), status codes and security schemes [OpenAPI Specification]. It grew out of Swagger and is maintained by the OpenAPI Initiative; version 3.1 aligned its schemas with JSON Schema, and version 3.2.0 was released in September 2025.

An OpenAPI document is the API’s contract in a form that tools can use: generating interactive documentation, client SDKs and server stubs, mock servers, request validation at gateways, and contract tests and breaking-change detection in CI (diffing the spec against the previous release flags the changes in Table 8.20 automatically).

openapi: 3.1.0
info:
  title: Articles API
  version: 1.0.0
paths:
  /v1/articles:
    get:
      summary: List articles, newest first
      parameters:
        - name: limit
          in: query
          schema: { type: integer, minimum: 1, maximum: 100, default: 20 }
        - name: cursor
          in: query
          description: Opaque cursor from a previous response's next_cursor.
          schema: { type: string }
      security:
        - bearerAuth: []
      responses:
        "200":
          description: A page of articles.
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: object
                required: [data, next_cursor]
                properties:
                  data:
                    type: array
                    items: { $ref: "#/components/schemas/Article" }
                  next_cursor: { type: [string, "null"] }
        "400":
          description: Invalid cursor.
          content:
            application/problem+json:
              schema: { $ref: "#/components/schemas/Problem" }
components:
  securitySchemes:
    bearerAuth: { type: http, scheme: bearer, bearerFormat: JWT }
  schemas:
    Article:
      type: object
      required: [id, title, status, created_at]
      properties:
        id: { type: integer }
        title: { type: string }
        status: { type: string, enum: [draft, published] }
        created_at: { type: string, format: date-time }
    Problem:
      type: object
      properties:
        type: { type: string, format: uri }
        title: { type: string }
        status: { type: integer }
        detail: { type: string }
        instance: { type: string }

What to notice: next_cursor is typed [string, "null"], OpenAPI 3.1’s JSON Schema way of saying “nullable”; errors are documented with the application/problem+json media type of §8.6.7; and the bearer scheme declares that operations need a JWT.

There are two workflows. In design-first, teams write and review the OpenAPI document before code, then generate stubs; this suits public APIs where the contract matters most. In code-first, the framework derives the document from code: FastAPI, for example, serves the document generated from the articles_api.py example of §8.6.5 at /openapi.json and interactive documentation at /docs, with no extra work. Either way, keep the spec in version control and treat changes to it as API changes that require review. GraphQL APIs are self-describing through introspection, and gRPC APIs through their .proto files, which play the same role.

8.17 Summary and revision notes

  • Client–server: clients initiate, servers own shared state. Keep the application tier stateless; state lives in databases, caches, cookies or tokens.
  • Rendering: SSR (server builds HTML), SPA (browser builds UI from JSON APIs), SSG (built once, served from a CDN), native mobile (old versions live for years). SPAs and mobile apps need a well-designed API; BFFs tailor it per client.
  • Lifecycle: DNS → TCP → TLS → load balancer → web server → app middleware → handler → cache/DB → response. On a cold connection, setup round trips often cost more than server work; reuse connections.
  • REST: resources named by URIs, standard methods, status codes. Know which methods are safe (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS) and idempotent (those plus PUT, DELETE). Make POST retryable with idempotency keys.
  • Pagination: offset costs O(offset+limit)O(\text{offset} + \text{limit}) and shifts under writes; cursor/keyset pagination with WHERE (sort_key, id) < (…) and a matching index is constant-cost and stable.
  • Errors: use status codes for the class of outcome and RFC 9457 application/problem+json for detail.
  • GraphQL: typed schema, client-chosen fields, one round trip. Fix N+1 with per-request DataLoader batching; HTTP caching is hard (use persisted queries); enforce depth and cost limits.
  • gRPC: Protobuf IDL, generated stubs, HTTP/2 streams; unary, server-, client- and bidirectional streaming. Always set and propagate deadlines; use L7 load balancing.
  • Serialization: JSON is readable and universal; Protobuf and Thrift use numeric tags and varints; Avro has no tags and resolves writer’s against reader’s schema. Evolve by adding optional fields with defaults; never reuse field numbers.
  • Cookies: Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax (or Strict), __Host- prefix. Sessions are server-side (instant revocation, one lookup) or signed cookies (no store, no early revocation).
  • AuthN vs AuthZ: who you are (401) vs what you may do (403). Hash passwords with slow salted functions (§10.6); prefer phishing-resistant MFA (WebAuthn/passkeys).
  • Authorization models: RBAC (roles), ABAC (attribute predicates), ReBAC (relationship graph; Zanzibar’s tuples, rewrites and zookies).
  • JWT: header.payload.signature, signed not encrypted. Pin the algorithm; validate exp, iss, aud. HS256 = shared secret; RS256/ES256 = private signs, public verifies. Revocation needs short TTLs, refresh tokens and/or deny-lists.
  • OAuth 2.0: delegated, scoped access via tokens. Use authorization code + PKCE for user-facing apps, client credentials for machines, rotating refresh tokens. OAuth 2.1 is still a draft (as of 2026). OIDC adds the ID token and standard login.
  • Versioning: additive changes need no new version; breaking changes do. URI, header, media-type or date-based pinning; deprecate with Deprecation/Sunset headers, usage metrics and brown-outs.
  • OpenAPI is the machine-readable contract: docs, SDKs, validation and breaking-change detection in CI.

8.18 Knowledge checkpoint

  1. Why does making the application tier stateless make horizontal scaling easy, and where does the state go?
  2. Name two backend consequences of supporting a native mobile client that an SSR website does not impose.
  3. A user 50 ms RTT away makes a first request needing an uncached DNS lookup (20 ms), TCP and TLS 1.3 setup, and 15 ms of server time. Estimate the latency, and the latency of the next request.
  4. Which HTTP methods are safe? Which are idempotent? Why does the distinction matter to a retry library?
  5. When should an API return 401, 403, 404, 409, 422 and 429?
  6. Write the keyset-pagination WHERE clause for sorting by created_at DESC, id DESC, and explain why id is included.
  7. Page size 50, page 10,001 with offset pagination: how many rows does the database walk? Roughly how many with keyset pagination?
  8. What are the five standard members of an RFC 9457 problem-details object?
  9. A GraphQL query fetches 20 posts and each post’s author. How many database queries run with naive resolvers and with DataLoader?
  10. Why must a DataLoader instance be created per request?
  11. What are the four gRPC call types? Give one use for each.
  12. What happens to a gRPC call with no deadline when the server hangs?
  13. Encode the integer 300 as a Protobuf varint in hex.
  14. In Protobuf, why must you never reuse a deleted field number? What does Avro need instead of field numbers?
  15. What does each of Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite=Lax protect against?
  16. Give one advantage and one disadvantage of a signed-cookie session versus a server-side session store.
  17. In a JWT, why must the server not use the alg value from the token header to choose the verification algorithm?
  18. Why does PKCE stop an attacker who intercepts the authorization code?
  19. What does OpenID Connect add to OAuth 2.0?
  20. Classify as breaking or non-breaking: adding an optional query parameter; renaming a response field; adding a required request field.
Answers
  1. Any instance can serve any request, so instances can be added, removed or replaced behind a load balancer without losing anything. State moves to databases, caches, a session store, or the client (cookies, tokens).
  2. Old app versions remain in use for months or years, so the API must stay backward compatible; slow cellular links make round trips expensive, favoring coarse-grained or aggregated endpoints (BFF, GraphQL) and compact payloads.
  3. Cold: 20+50+50+50+15=18520 + 50 + 50 + 50 + 15 = 185 ms. Next request on the same connection with cached DNS: 50+15=6550 + 15 = 65 ms.
  4. Safe: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS (and TRACE). Idempotent: the safe methods plus PUT and DELETE. A retry library can automatically retry idempotent requests after a timeout; retrying POST may duplicate effects unless an idempotency key is used.
  5. 401: not authenticated. 403: authenticated but not permitted. 404: no such resource (or hidden). 409: conflicts with current state, such as a duplicate key. 422: well-formed but semantically invalid input. 429: rate limit exceeded, with Retry-After.
  6. WHERE (created_at, id) < (:last_created_at, :last_id) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT :n. id makes the order total, so rows sharing a timestamp are neither skipped nor repeated across pages.
  7. Offset =10,000×50=500,000= 10{,}000 \times 50 = 500{,}000, so about 500,050 rows. Keyset: an index descent (~3–4 levels) plus 50–51 rows.
  8. type, title, status, detail, instance.
  9. Naive: 1+20=211 + 20 = 21. DataLoader: 2 (one for posts, one batched IN query for distinct authors).
  10. Its cache would otherwise serve one user’s data (possibly unauthorized) to another user and return stale data across requests.
  11. Unary (fetch an order); server streaming (status updates, tailing logs); client streaming (uploading telemetry in chunks); bidirectional (chat, live transcription).
  12. The client waits indefinitely, holding a thread or connection and memory; under load such calls accumulate and can exhaust the caller, cascading up the call chain.
  13. 300 = 1 0010 1100. Low 7 bits 010 1100 = 0x2C, plus continuation bit → ac; remaining bits 10 → 02. Result: ac 02.
  14. Old data or old clients would interpret the new field’s bytes as the old field, causing silent corruption. Avro needs the writer’s schema (from a file header or schema registry) and resolves fields by name, using defaults.
  15. Secure: leakage over unencrypted HTTP. HttpOnly: theft of the cookie by JavaScript injected through XSS. SameSite=Lax: the cookie being sent on cross-site POSTs and subresource requests, that is, CSRF.
  16. Advantage: no store lookup and no shared infrastructure. Disadvantage: cannot be revoked individually before expiry; limited to ~4 KB sent on every request; contents readable by the user.
  17. An attacker controls the header. They could set alg: none, or HS256 and sign with the server’s public RSA key as the HMAC secret (algorithm confusion). The server must use its configured algorithm allow-list.
  18. The code is useless without the code verifier, which never travels through the browser; only its SHA-256 hash does, and the hash cannot be inverted.
  19. A standard identity layer: the openid scope, the ID token (a JWT about the authenticated user with audience = client), the UserInfo endpoint, standard claims, nonce-based replay protection and discovery metadata.
  20. Non-breaking; breaking; breaking.

8.19 Interview questions

Basic

Q1. Walk me through what happens when a user types a URL and presses Enter. Answer. The browser parses the URL and checks its HTTP cache. It resolves the host name through DNS (OS cache, then recursive resolver, then authoritative servers), opens a TCP connection (one RTT) and performs a TLS 1.3 handshake (one RTT), or a combined QUIC handshake on HTTP/3. It sends the HTTP request with headers and cookies. A load balancer terminates TLS, routes on host and path, and forwards to a healthy backend over a pooled connection. The web server passes it to the application, where middleware authenticates, rate-limits and routes to a handler; the handler authorizes, reads cache and database, serializes a response and returns it back through the chain. The browser parses and renders, fetching subresources, often over the same connection. Strong answers attach rough numbers to each hop and note which steps connection reuse and CDNs remove.

Q2. What is the difference between PUT, PATCH and POST? Answer. POST asks the target collection or resource to process the body, commonly creating a resource whose URI the server chooses; it is not idempotent. PUT creates or completely replaces the resource at the URI the client names; it is idempotent. PATCH applies a partial modification; it is not guaranteed idempotent (an “increment” patch is not). Retries are therefore safe for PUT but need idempotency keys for POST.

Q3. Cookies or tokens for authentication? Answer. For a first-party browser application, an opaque session ID in a Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite cookie is simple and secure and allows instant logout. For APIs consumed by mobile apps, other services or third parties, short-lived bearer tokens (often JWTs) obtained through OAuth fit better, because any service can verify them without a shared store. Many systems combine them: the browser holds a session cookie with a BFF, which holds tokens and calls services with them.

Intermediate

Q4. Design pagination for an activity feed API with 500 million rows and constant inserts. Answer. Use cursor (keyset) pagination ordered by (created_at DESC, id DESC), backed by a composite index (per user, if the feed is per user: (user_id, created_at DESC, id DESC)). The response returns data and an opaque next_cursor encoding the last row’s sort key, base64url-encoded and HMAC-signed, optionally with an expiry and a hash of the filter parameters. Query with a row-value comparison and LIMIT n+1 to detect more pages. Cap limit at, say, 100. Omit total counts or serve approximate ones. Explain why offset fails: cost grows linearly with depth (deep pages walk millions of rows) and inserts cause duplicates. Mention that cursors survive deletes of the boundary row because the comparison is on values, not on row existence.

Q5. Your GraphQL API’s database load tripled after a new mobile screen launched. Diagnose and fix. Answer. Likely N+1 resolution on nested lists, possibly compounded by a query requesting large page sizes or deep nesting. Confirm with per-request query counts and resolver tracing. Fix with per-request DataLoaders for every relation field (batch by parent IDs, dedupe), enforce maximum first values, add query-cost analysis with per-client budgets, and use persisted queries so the expensive query can be reviewed and cached. Consider caching hot entities in the batch functions.

Q6. How do you revoke access for a user whose laptop was stolen, if your APIs use JWT access tokens? Answer. Revoke their refresh tokens at the authorization server (so no new access tokens are minted) and end their server-side sessions. For outstanding access tokens, either accept exposure until expiry (keep TTLs at 5–15 minutes) or push a deny-list entry — by jti, or “all tokens for sub issued before T” — to a replicated store or in-memory cache in every resource server, checked during validation. Entries can expire with the tokens, so the list stays small. High-risk operations can additionally require introspection or step-up authentication.

Advanced

Q7. Design authorization for a document-collaboration product with folders, nested groups and link sharing, serving 100,000 checks per second at p99 under 20 ms. Answer. Use ReBAC in the Zanzibar style. Store tuples object#relation@subject (subjects can be usersets like group:eng#member) in a partitioned, replicated store, partitioned by object ID. Define namespace rewrite rules: owner ⊂ editor ⊂ commenter ⊂ viewer, and viewer inherited from parent folder; link sharing is a tuple with a special subject such as anyone-with-link. A check service evaluates the rewrite graph with memoization of sub-results, request deduplication, depth limits and a precomputed membership index for large nested groups. For freshness, return a consistency token with each ACL or content write and evaluate later checks at a snapshot at least that recent, avoiding the new-enemy problem; otherwise allow slightly stale cached results for latency. Provide list/filter APIs (“which of these 50 docs can Alice see?”) as batched checks. Discuss failure modes: the authorization service on every read path must be multi-region and degrade by failing closed; audit logs of tuple changes; and the cost of deep nesting.

Q8. Your company runs 300 microservices with a mix of REST/JSON and gRPC. Propose an inter-service API strategy, including versioning and schema evolution. Answer. Default to gRPC with Protobuf for internal synchronous calls: compact, typed, streaming, deadline propagation. Keep all .proto files in a central schema repository with linting and breaking-change detection in CI; version by package (orders.v1), additive changes only within a version. Expose public and partner APIs as REST/JSON with OpenAPI, generated or transcoded from the same definitions where possible, with RFC 9457 errors and date-based or major-version URIs. Mandate deadlines on every call, propagation of deadline and trace context, and status-code-based retry policies with budgets. Use L7 or client-side load balancing for HTTP/2. For asynchronous events, use Avro or Protobuf with a schema registry enforcing backward/forward compatibility. Measure the usage of every deprecated field and method before removal.

Q9. Walk through the security of a SPA that signs users in with an external identity provider and calls your API. Answer. The SPA is a public client, so use the authorization code flow with PKCE (S256), a random state, and an OIDC nonce; register exact redirect URIs. Preferably run a BFF: the browser holds only an HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax (or Strict), __Host- session cookie with the BFF, which performs the code exchange as a confidential client and stores access and refresh tokens server-side, so XSS cannot steal tokens. Validate the ID token (signature via JWKS, iss, aud = client ID, exp, nonce) and identify users by (iss, sub). The API validates access tokens with pinned algorithms, aud = API, scopes, and short TTLs; refresh tokens rotate with reuse detection. Add CSRF protection for state-changing BFF endpoints, a strict Content Security Policy, and an authorization check on every object access.

8.20 Practical exercises

  1. Build a small REST API (2–4 h). Extend articles_api.py (§8.6.5) into a FastAPI or Flask service backed by SQLite or PostgreSQL with POST /v1/articles (201 + Location), GET with cursor pagination and filtering by status and author_id, PATCH with If-Match ETags (412 on mismatch), and DELETE (204). Protect writes with the JWT dependency of §8.13.3 and scopes articles:write and articles:delete. Return RFC 9457 errors throughout. Write tests that page through 1,000 rows while inserting new ones, and assert that no row is returned twice.
  2. Measure offset versus keyset. Load 5 million rows into PostgreSQL. Time OFFSET queries at offsets 0, 10⁴, 10⁵ and 10⁶, and the equivalent keyset queries, and read EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) for each. Plot latency against page depth.
  3. Encode by hand. Write a decoder for the varint encoder of §8.9.2 that turns the 33-byte message back into fields, skipping unknown field numbers using the wire type. Add sint64 ZigZag support and verify against the official protobuf library.
  4. Fix an N+1. Implement the blog schema of §8.7.1 with Strawberry or Ariadne (Python) over SQLite, log every SQL statement, and count queries for a request of 50 posts with comments and authors. Add DataLoaders and compare.
  5. OAuth end to end. Run an open-source identity provider (for example Keycloak) locally, register a public client, and implement the authorization code + PKCE flow from a small Python web app, including state, nonce and ID-token validation. Then demonstrate that replaying a stolen code without the verifier fails.

8.21 Design challenges

  1. Public API for a payments startup. Design the external API for creating charges, refunds and listing transactions: resource model, idempotency keys, pagination, error types, webhooks, authentication for merchants (API keys vs OAuth for platforms), versioning and deprecation policy. Justify every status code.
  2. One backend, three frontends. A retailer has an SSR website, an iOS/Android app with five live versions, and partner integrations. Choose between REST, GraphQL, BFFs and gRPC for each layer, draw the architecture, and explain how a schema change to “product price” rolls out without breaking any client.
  3. Authorization at scale. A B2B SaaS product needs per-tenant roles, per-project sharing and conditional rules (“contractors only from the corporate network”). Combine RBAC, ReBAC and ABAC; specify the data model, the check API, caching and consistency, and how you would audit “who can see project X?”.

Chapter 9 — Real-Time Communication

Level: 2 · Track: A (Traditional) · Estimated reading time: 3 h

The web was built as a conversation in which only one side may speak first. A browser asks; a server answers; the exchange ends. That model, described in §8.5 (The request–response lifecycle), works well for loading a page or submitting a form. It works badly when the server is the first to know something: a new chat message has arrived, a stock price has moved, a driver is two minutes away, a colleague has started typing. This chapter is about the family of techniques that let a server tell a client about something now, without waiting to be asked.

Picture a restaurant kitchen and a diner. Short polling is the diner walking to the kitchen every five minutes to ask “is my food ready?”. Long polling is the diner asking once and the chef saying “wait here, I’ll tell you as soon as it is”. Server-Sent Events is a waiter assigned to the diner’s table who walks over every time a course is ready. WebSockets is a telephone line between table and kitchen that either side can talk into at any moment. WebRTC lets two diners talk to each other directly across the room instead of passing notes through the kitchen. Mobile push is the restaurant sending a text message to a diner who has gone home: the phone company decides when it arrives, and it might not arrive at all. Every technique in this chapter is a trade between how quickly the news arrives, how much it costs to keep the line open, and how much infrastructure must understand the line.

9.1 Learning objectives

After this chapter you should be able to:

  • Explain the mechanism, wire format and failure modes of short polling, long polling, Server-Sent Events (SSE), WebSockets, WebRTC and mobile push.
  • Calculate the request rate, wasted requests and added latency of a polling design from the number of clients and the polling interval.
  • Walk through the RFC 6455 WebSocket opening handshake, compute Sec-WebSocket-Accept, and decode a WebSocket frame byte by byte, including masking.
  • Describe how ICE, STUN and TURN establish a peer-to-peer WebRTC session, and choose between mesh, SFU and MCU topologies with bandwidth arithmetic.
  • Design a mobile push pipeline using APNs and FCM that tolerates dropped notifications, stale device tokens and collapsed messages.
  • Size a connection gateway fleet for 10 million concurrent connections, including memory, server count, heartbeat load and reconnect-storm behavior.
  • Design a pub/sub backplane, a presence system and a graceful-drain deployment procedure for long-lived connections.
  • Choose the right real-time technique for a given product requirement and defend the choice with a comparison of cost, latency and operational complexity.

9.2 Prerequisites

  • TCP connections, the three-way handshake and head-of-line blocking — §7.7 (needed because every technique here rides on long-lived TCP or UDP flows).
  • HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and QUIC — §7.9 (SSE and WebSockets interact with HTTP versions in non-obvious ways).
  • TLS 1.3 — §7.10 (handshake cost dominates reconnect storms).
  • WebSockets introduction — §7.11 (this chapter is the deep dive).
  • Proxies, reverse proxies and NAT — §7.12, §7.13 (they break long-lived connections and motivate STUN/TURN).
  • I/O models and event loops (epoll, kqueue, async/await) — §6.13, §6.15 (how one server holds hundreds of thousands of idle connections).
  • Little’s Law — §4.11 (concurrent connections = arrival rate × connection lifetime).
  • Load balancing and session affinity — §19.3, §19.6 (sticky routing for connections).
  • Retries with exponential backoff and jitter — §22.12 (reconnect storms).

9.3 Short polling

9.3.1 What short polling is

Definition — Short polling. A technique in which the client sends an ordinary HTTP request at a fixed interval T to ask whether new data exists; the server answers immediately, either with the new data or with an empty response, and the connection’s request ends.

First-principles explanation

A child in the back seat asking “are we there yet?” every minute is short polling. The parent answers right away, almost always with “no”. The child learns of arrival at most one minute late, and the parent spends most of the trip answering a question whose answer has not changed. Nothing about the car or the road had to change to support this protocol, which is precisely why it is popular.

Why does this exist?

Short polling needs nothing beyond what every HTTP client, proxy, CDN, firewall and load balancer already supports. It was the first way web pages showed “live” data, and it remains the right answer when updates are infrequent, a few seconds of staleness is acceptable and clients are few — a build-status page polled every 30 seconds by a few hundred engineers, for example.

How it works internally

  1. The client starts a timer with period T (for example, 5 seconds).
  2. When the timer fires, the client sends GET /updates?since=<cursor>. The cursor is an opaque value (a sequence number or timestamp) identifying the last item the client has seen.
  3. The server looks up anything newer than the cursor and responds immediately: 200 OK with items and a new cursor, or 204 No Content (or 200 with an empty list, or 304 Not Modified with an ETag) when nothing changed.
  4. The client applies the items, stores the new cursor and waits for the next tick.
  5. With HTTP keep-alive (§7.16), the TCP and TLS connection is reused across polls, so each poll costs one request/response round trip rather than a full handshake.

Architecture diagram

Figure 9.1 — Short polling.

Reading the diagram. The client, a stateless API server and the data store exchange only synchronous HTTP over a reused keep-alive connection (solid = request, dashed = response); the server never initiates. Event 42 is written between polls, so the client learns of it up to T seconds late — inherent, not a bug. The data store receives one read per poll whether or not anything changed, which is the failure point at scale. Scaling is easy: stateless servers behind a load balancer, with a cache in front of the “anything new?” query.

Mathematical foundations

Short-polling request rate

R=NTR = \frac{N}{T}

Symbol Meaning Units
RR Request rate arriving at the servers requests/second
NN Number of concurrently active (polling) clients clients
TT Polling interval seconds

Fraction of wasted (empty) polls and added latency

If updates for a client arrive as a Poisson process with rate λ\lambda, the probability that a given interval contains no update is

Pempty=e−λT≈1−λT(when λT≪1)P_{\text{empty}} = e^{-\lambda T} \approx 1 - \lambda T \quad (\text{when } \lambda T \ll 1)

and the average delay between an event occurring and the client seeing it is

Davg=T2+trttD_{\text{avg}} = \frac{T}{2} + t_{\text{rtt}}

Symbol Meaning Units
PemptyP_{\text{empty}} Fraction of polls that return nothing dimensionless (0–1)
λ\lambda Average update rate per client events/second
TT Polling interval seconds
DavgD_{\text{avg}} Average notification delay seconds
trttt_{\text{rtt}} Network round-trip time for one poll seconds

Worked example — A notification badge polled every 5 seconds.

A web app has N=1,000,000N = 1{,}000{,}000 users online at peak. Each tab polls /notifications every T=5T = 5 s. A typical user receives one notification every 10 minutes, so λ=1/600≈0.00167\lambda = 1/600 \approx 0.00167 events/s.

  1. Request rate: R=1,000,000/5=200,000R = 1{,}000{,}000 / 5 = 200{,}000 requests/s.
  2. Empty fraction: λT=5/600=0.00833\lambda T = 5/600 = 0.00833; Pempty=e−0.00833≈0.9917P_{\text{empty}} = e^{-0.00833} \approx 0.9917. So 99.2 % of requests — about 198,300 per second — return nothing.
  3. Useful requests: 200,000×0.0083≈1,700200{,}000 \times 0.0083 \approx 1{,}700 per second actually carry a notification.
  4. Header overhead: assume about 800 bytes of request headers (cookies, user-agent, auth token) and 200 bytes of response headers on HTTP/1.1 — about 1 KB per poll (SI units, 1 KB = 1,000 bytes). 200,000×1 KB=200200{,}000 \times 1\text{ KB} = 200 MB/s ≈ 1.6 Gbit/s of traffic that mostly says “nothing new”. HTTP/2 header compression (HPACK) shrinks repeated headers considerably, but the request count and server work remain.
  5. Average delay: Davg≈2.5D_{\text{avg}} \approx 2.5 s plus one round trip.

Interpretation. You are paying for 200,000 requests per second of capacity — load balancers, TLS termination, application threads and a database or cache lookup each — to deliver about 1,700 useful updates per second. Halving the interval to 2.5 s to improve freshness doubles the bill.

Engineering implication. Short polling’s cost scales with N/TN/T, not with the rate of real events. When λT\lambda T is small (rare events, short interval), switch to a push technique; when events are frequent relative to the interval (for example, a dashboard that changes every second and is polled every 10 s), polling’s waste is low and its simplicity wins.

Table 9.1 — Short-polling cost for 1 million clients as the interval shrinks (λ = 1 event per 10 minutes per client).

Interval TT Requests/s Empty polls Avg. delay Header traffic (≈1 KB/poll)
60 s 16,667 90.5 % 30 s 16.7 MB/s
30 s 33,333 95.1 % 15 s 33.3 MB/s
10 s 100,000 98.3 % 5 s 100 MB/s
5 s 200,000 99.2 % 2.5 s 200 MB/s
1 s 1,000,000 99.8 % 0.5 s 1 GB/s

The table shows the central tension: every halving of delay doubles the cost, while the useful work stays constant at about 1,667 notifications per second.

Real-world industry applications

Status dashboards and job progress pages. A CI system’s build page or a cloud console’s “creating instance…” spinner typically polls a status endpoint every few seconds. The number of watchers is small, staleness of a few seconds is invisible to users, and the endpoint can be served from a cache, so the waste is cheap and the operational simplicity (no long-lived connections, works through every proxy) dominates. Evidence: Illustrative — a common pattern used for teaching; not a claim about any specific product.

Advantages and disadvantages

  • Advantages: works everywhere (every proxy, CDN, firewall, HTTP version); servers stay stateless; trivially cacheable (ETag, Cache-Control: max-age); easy to rate-limit and to reason about; failures are self-healing because the next poll simply retries.
  • Disadvantages: latency is bounded below by T/2T/2 on average; cost grows with clients and polling frequency rather than with real events; mobile radios are woken on every poll, draining battery; synchronized clients (for example, all tabs opened at 09:00) create load spikes unless the timer is jittered.

Alternatives and trade-offs

Long polling (§9.4) removes empty responses and the T/2T/2 delay; SSE (§9.5) and WebSockets (§9.6) remove per-update request overhead. Adaptive polling — lengthening TT while nothing changes, or honoring a server-supplied Retry-After hint — is a cheap middle ground.

Failure scenarios

Table 9.2 — Short-polling failure scenarios.

What goes wrong Why Detection Recovery Prevention
Synchronized poll spikes Clients start timers at the same moment (deploy, page load at shift start) Request-rate graph shows sawtooth at multiples of TT Shed load with 429 + Retry-After Add ±20 % random jitter to every timer
Database overload Every empty poll hits the database DB CPU tracks request rate, not write rate Cache “latest cursor per user” in memory Serve “anything new?” from a cache or version counter
Missed updates Client uses wall-clock timestamps as cursor; clock skew or same-millisecond writes Users report gaps Re-fetch from an earlier cursor Use monotonically increasing sequence numbers

Common misconceptions

“Polling every second is fine; requests are cheap.” A request that returns nothing still costs a TLS record, a load-balancer decision, an application thread slot, an authentication check and usually a cache or database lookup. Multiplied by N/TN/T, “cheap” becomes the dominant load on the system. Always compute R=N/TR = N/T before choosing an interval.

9.4 Long polling

9.4.1 What long polling is

Definition — Long polling. A technique in which the client sends an HTTP request that the server deliberately does not answer until either new data is available or a server-side timeout Thold expires; on receiving any response, the client immediately sends the next request.

First-principles explanation

Now the child asks once and the parent says “I’ll tell you when we arrive — and if nothing happens in half an hour I’ll say so anyway”. The news arrives the instant it happens, but the parent must remember that a question is pending — that memory is the new cost.

Why does this exist?

Mid-2000s webmail and chat needed sub-second updates, but browsers could only make JavaScript-initiated HTTP requests. Nothing in HTTP forbids a server from answering slowly, so holding the request open approximates push using only standard HTTP. Alex Russell named this family of techniques Comet in 2006 [Russell 2006]; the CometD project’s Bayeux protocol standardized a message format, and RFC 6202 documented the pitfalls [Loreto et al. 2011]. Long polling survives as the universal fallback transport in libraries such as Socket.IO.

How it works internally

  1. The client sends GET /poll?cursor=41.
  2. The server checks for items after cursor 41. If any exist, it responds immediately (this is exactly short polling’s fast path).
  3. If none exist, the server parks the request in an in-memory waiter list keyed by user or topic. On an event-loop server (§6.13) a parked request costs only memory, not a thread.
  4. When an event for that user arrives from a broker, the server wakes the waiter and responds with the new items and cursor.
  5. If no event arrives within Thold (commonly 20–55 seconds), the server responds 204 No Content or an empty list with the same cursor.
  6. On any response the client immediately re-polls with the latest cursor (after a backoff delay if the response was an error).

Timeouts. Thold must be shorter than every idle timeout on the path. The AWS Application Load Balancer’s default idle timeout is 60 s and NGINX’s proxy_read_timeout defaults to 60 s (as of 2024); corporate proxies may be shorter, so 25–30 s is a common safe choice. If an intermediary cuts the request first, the client sees an error instead of a clean empty response — and if it retries without backoff, an error storm.

Ordering and loss. Between response k and request k+1 there is a one-round-trip gap with no outstanding request. The cursor closes it: the server keeps a per-user buffer of recent events with monotonically increasing sequence numbers, and each request asks for “everything after c”. Clients apply items in sequence order and discard duplicates (an event racing a timeout may be sent twice). Never run two concurrent long polls per client: responses can arrive out of order. A parked request also occupies one of the browser’s roughly six HTTP/1.1 connections per origin [Loreto et al. 2011].

Architecture diagram

Figure 9.2 — Long polling with cursors and a hold timeout.

Reading the diagram. The poll server receives events asynchronously (open arrowheads) from a pub/sub broker. The first request parks and ends empty after the 30 s hold timeout; the second is answered the moment event 42 arrives — one network hop instead of T/2T/2. Event 43 arrives while the client is re-polling; the cursor and the server-side buffer ensure nothing is lost. If the client reconnects to a different server, that server must answer “after 42”, so the buffer must be shared or routing sticky (§9.9.4). Failure points: intermediaries that time out first, and in-memory buffers lost on restart. Capacity is planned in concurrent held connections.

Mathematical foundations

Long-polling request rate

With Poisson events at rate λ\lambda per client and hold timeout ThT_h, each request lasts min(Th,X)\min(T_h, X) where XX is the time to the next event. Its mean is

E[duration]=1−e−λThλ,R=NE[duration],Copen≈NE[\text{duration}] = \frac{1 - e^{-\lambda T_h}}{\lambda}, \qquad R = \frac{N}{E[\text{duration}]}, \qquad C_{\text{open}} \approx N

Symbol Meaning Units
λ\lambda Average update rate per client events/second
ThT_h Server hold timeout seconds
E[duration]E[\text{duration}] Mean lifetime of one long-poll request seconds
NN Number of connected clients clients
RR Request rate at the servers requests/second
CopenC_{\text{open}} Concurrently open requests (Little’s Law: R×E[duration]R \times E[\text{duration}]) requests

Worked example — The same 1 million users, now with long polling.

Use the numbers from §9.3: N=1,000,000N = 1{,}000{,}000, λ=1/600\lambda = 1/600 events/s, and a hold timeout Th=30T_h = 30 s.

  1. λTh=30/600=0.05\lambda T_h = 30/600 = 0.05; e−0.05=0.9512e^{-0.05} = 0.9512.
  2. E[duration]=(1−0.9512)/(1/600)=0.0488×600≈29.3E[\text{duration}] = (1 - 0.9512) / (1/600) = 0.0488 \times 600 \approx 29.3 s.
  3. R=1,000,000/29.3≈34,000R = 1{,}000{,}000 / 29.3 \approx 34{,}000 requests/s, versus 200,000 requests/s for 5-second short polling — about 5.9× fewer requests.
  4. Average notification delay: about one network round trip (tens of milliseconds) instead of 2.5 s.
  5. Concurrent open requests: 34,000×29.3≈1,000,00034{,}000 \times 29.3 \approx 1{,}000{,}000 — every client holds one open request at all times.

Interpretation. Long polling improves both cost and latency, but it shifts the bottleneck from request throughput to concurrent held connections. 95 % of responses are still empty timeouts (e−0.05e^{-0.05}), each carrying full HTTP headers.

Engineering implication. Long polling needs an asynchronous server that can park a million requests and an event-routing layer that wakes the right one — the same infrastructure as a WebSocket gateway (§9.9). Once you have built that, SSE or WebSockets usually deliver more for the same effort.

Real-world industry applications

Universal fallback transports. Real-time libraries such as Socket.IO and SockJS offer long polling as a transport for networks where WebSockets are blocked by proxies or firewalls. Socket.IO’s documentation notes that when HTTP long-polling is enabled with several server nodes, the load balancer must use sticky sessions, because successive polls of one session must reach the node that holds its state. Evidence: Primary — Socket.IO documentation, “Using multiple nodes” [Socket.IO Docs].

Advantages and disadvantages

  • Advantages: near-instant delivery over plain HTTP; works through almost every proxy; client logic is simple; degrades to polling when events are frequent.
  • Disadvantages: every message still carries full HTTP headers and costs a new request; a round-trip gap after each response (mitigated by cursors); holds a connection per client, so servers must be asynchronous; intermediary timeouts must be understood; occupies one of the browser’s HTTP/1.1 connections per origin; strictly server-to-client (client-to-server messages need separate requests).

Alternatives and trade-offs

SSE (§9.5) gives the same reach for server-to-client data with one request for many messages and built-in resumption; WebSockets (§9.6) remove per-message HTTP overhead for bidirectional traffic. Long polling wins where streaming responses are broken — some antivirus products and corporate proxies buffer responses until they complete, which ruins SSE but leaves long polling intact.

Failure scenarios

Table 9.3 — Long-polling failure scenarios.

What goes wrong Why Detection Recovery Prevention
Requests cut off at 60 s with 504 Hold timeout exceeds a proxy or LB idle timeout Spike in 504/502 at exactly the intermediary’s timeout Lower hold timeout Keep hold timeout below the smallest idle timeout on the path
Lost events Server buffers in memory and restarts; client lands on another node Sequence gaps detected by client Client resyncs with a full fetch Shared event store or sticky routing plus resync-on-gap
Retry storm Clients re-poll instantly after errors Request rate jumps far above N/ThN/T_h Shed with 503 + Retry-After Exponential backoff with jitter on errors (§22.12)

Common misconceptions

“Long polling is just polling with a longer interval.” No — the interval is not a client timer at all. The server decides when to answer, so delivery latency is one hop, not T/2T/2. What it shares with polling is the per-message HTTP cost and the reconnect after every response.

9.5 Server-Sent Events

9.5.1 What SSE is

Definition — Server-Sent Events (SSE). A W3C/WHATWG-standardized mechanism in which a client opens one long-lived HTTP request and the server streams a sequence of UTF-8 text events down the response body using the text/event-stream format; browsers expose it through the EventSource API, which parses events and reconnects automatically, resuming from the last received event ID [WHATWG HTML §9.2].

First-principles explanation

Long polling is like ordering a newspaper one issue at a time: each issue arrives, and then you must place the next order. SSE is a newspaper subscription: you sign up once and issues keep arriving at your door. If you move house (the connection drops), you tell the newspaper “the last issue I received was number 1,042”, and they send you everything from 1,043 onward.

Why does this exist?

Long polling wastes a full request per message. Many features need only server-to-client data: feeds, notifications, live scores, progress bars, and the token-by-token output of large language models (Chapter 73). SSE standardizes “keep the response open and keep writing”, adds a tiny text framing, and builds reconnection and resumption into the browser.

How it works internally

  1. The client creates new EventSource("/events") (optionally { withCredentials: true } for cross-origin cookies). The browser sends GET /events with Accept: text/event-stream.
  2. The server responds 200 OK with Content-Type: text/event-stream and Cache-Control: no-cache, then does not end the response. It writes events as they occur.
  3. Each event is a block of field: value lines terminated by a blank line. The fields are:
    • data: — the payload; several data: lines are joined with newline characters.
    • event: — an event type; the browser dispatches it to listeners registered with addEventListener("<type>", …); without it the event fires onmessage.
    • id: — sets the stream’s last event ID.
    • retry: — an integer in milliseconds; sets the reconnection delay.
    • A line beginning with : is a comment, ignored by the parser — servers send one every 15–30 seconds as a heartbeat to stop intermediaries from closing an idle connection.
  4. If the connection drops because of a network error, the browser waits the reconnection time (initially an implementation-defined value of a few seconds, or whatever retry: set) and re-sends the request with a Last-Event-ID header containing the last id: it received. The server replays events after that ID from a buffer and then continues live.
  5. The server can stop reconnection permanently by responding 204 No Content. A response with a status other than 200, or a wrong Content-Type, makes the browser fail the connection rather than retry — so a load balancer returning 503 during an outage silently turns off auto-reconnect, and your application code must notice (readyState === EventSource.CLOSED) and recreate the EventSource with backoff.

A stream on the wire looks like this:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/event-stream
Cache-Control: no-cache

retry: 5000

: heartbeat

id: 1042
event: price
data: {"symbol":"ACME","price":101.25}

id: 1043
event: price
data: {"symbol":"ACME","price":101.40}

Interaction with HTTP versions. Over HTTP/1.1 each EventSource holds a whole TCP connection, and browsers allow only about six HTTP/1.1 connections per origin across all tabs, so a seventh tab can stall. Over HTTP/2 (§7.9) each stream is multiplexed on one shared connection, limited by the server’s SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS (commonly 100 or more), and a new stream needs no TCP or TLS handshake; the price is TCP head-of-line blocking across all streams, which HTTP/3 removes. Finally, reverse proxies that buffer responses (NGINX does by default) hold events back: disable buffering on stream routes (proxy_buffering off; or the header X-Accel-Buffering: no) and keep compression middleware off them.

Architecture diagram

Figure 9.3 — SSE streaming, disconnection and resumption with Last-Event-ID.

Reading the diagram. Every dashed arrow from the server is a chunk of the same streamed response. After a network failure the browser reconnects by itself with Last-Event-ID; the load balancer may pick a different server, which is why the event buffer (Redis Streams, Kafka, a replicated ring) lives outside the SSE server. Data flows only server-to-client; client actions use ordinary HTTP requests. Failure points: buffering proxies, idle timeouts on silent streams (fixed by heartbeat comments), and a buffer that no longer reaches back to the client’s ID (force a full resync). SSE servers scale like the gateways in §9.9.

Code example

The following SSE endpoint uses only the Python standard library and has been run and tested with curl -N. It keeps a bounded history so that reconnecting clients resume from Last-Event-ID.

"""Minimal Server-Sent Events endpoint using only the standard library.

Run:   python3 sse_server.py
Test:  curl -N http://127.0.0.1:8080/events
       curl -N -H "Last-Event-ID: 3" http://127.0.0.1:8080/events
"""
import asyncio
import json
import time

HISTORY: list[tuple[int, str]] = []    # (event id, JSON payload) ring buffer
HISTORY_LIMIT = 1000
new_event = asyncio.Condition()

async def producer() -> None:
    """Pretend to be a business event source: one price tick per second."""
    event_id = 0
    while True:
        await asyncio.sleep(1)
        event_id += 1
        payload = json.dumps({"symbol": "ACME", "price": 100 + event_id, "ts": time.time()})
        async with new_event:
            HISTORY.append((event_id, payload))
            del HISTORY[:-HISTORY_LIMIT]          # keep the buffer bounded
            new_event.notify_all()

def format_event(event_id: int, data: str) -> bytes:
    return f"id: {event_id}\nevent: price\ndata: {data}\n\n".encode()

async def handle(reader: asyncio.StreamReader, writer: asyncio.StreamWriter) -> None:
    # 1. Read the request line and headers (no body for GET).
    request_line = await reader.readline()
    headers = {}
    while (line := await reader.readline()) not in (b"\r\n", b"\n", b""):
        name, _, value = line.decode().partition(":")
        headers[name.strip().lower()] = value.strip()
    if not request_line.startswith(b"GET /events"):
        writer.write(b"HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found\r\nContent-Length: 0\r\n\r\n")
        await writer.drain(); writer.close(); return

    # 2. Resume point: the browser sends Last-Event-ID automatically on reconnect.
    try:
        last_seen = int(headers.get("last-event-id", "0"))
    except ValueError:
        last_seen = 0

    writer.write(b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\n"
                 b"Content-Type: text/event-stream\r\n"
                 b"Cache-Control: no-cache\r\n"
                 b"Connection: keep-alive\r\n\r\n"
                 b"retry: 5000\n\n")          # ask client to wait 5 s before reconnecting
    try:
        while True:
            # 3. Send everything newer than last_seen (replay, then live).
            pending = [(i, d) for i, d in HISTORY if i > last_seen]
            for event_id, data in pending:
                writer.write(format_event(event_id, data))
                last_seen = event_id
            if not pending:
                writer.write(b": keep-alive\n\n")   # comment line; defeats idle timeouts
            await writer.drain()                    # backpressure: wait if socket buffer full
            async with new_event:
                try:
                    await asyncio.wait_for(new_event.wait(), timeout=15)
                except asyncio.TimeoutError:
                    pass
    except (ConnectionResetError, BrokenPipeError):
        pass
    finally:
        writer.close()

async def main() -> None:
    asyncio.create_task(producer())
    server = await asyncio.start_server(handle, "127.0.0.1", 8080)
    async with server:
        await server.serve_forever()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

On the browser side, consuming this stream takes four lines:

const es = new EventSource("/events");
es.addEventListener("price", (e) => render(JSON.parse(e.data)));
es.onerror = () => { if (es.readyState === EventSource.CLOSED) scheduleRecreate(); };
// the browser reconnects by itself after network errors and sends Last-Event-ID

What to notice:

  • The response never ends; the server writes id:/event:/data: blocks separated by blank lines. Curl started with -H "Last-Event-ID: 2" received events 3, 4, 5… — the replay-then-live behavior the browser gets for free.
  • await writer.drain() is the backpressure point: if a client reads slowly, the coroutine pauses instead of letting the process buffer unbounded data (§9.6.7).
  • The : keep-alive comment is invisible to EventSource but keeps proxies and load balancers from closing an idle connection.
  • The in-memory HISTORY would be lost on restart and is not shared between servers; production systems put it in Redis Streams, Kafka or a database so any server can replay.

Real-world industry applications

Streaming responses from large-language-model APIs. Several widely used LLM HTTP APIs stream generated tokens to clients as text/event-stream responses, because generation is strictly one-directional (server to client), each response is short-lived (seconds to minutes), and SSE passes through standard HTTP infrastructure, authentication and rate limiting unchanged. Chapter 73 discusses time to first token (TTFT) and inter-token latency (ITL), which is what this streaming exposes to users. Evidence: Illustrative — a widely observed pattern; consult each provider’s API documentation for specifics.

Advantages and disadvantages

  • Advantages: plain HTTP (works with existing auth, cookies, CORS, load balancers, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3); automatic reconnection and resumption built into browsers; tiny per-event framing (tens of bytes); simple to implement on any server that can flush a response; easy to debug with curl -N.
  • Disadvantages: server-to-client only; UTF-8 text only (binary must be base64-encoded, +33 %); the standard EventSource cannot set custom request headers (use cookies, a short-lived token in the URL, or a fetch-based stream reader instead); HTTP/1.1 connection-per-origin limits; buffering proxies and compression can delay events; non-200 responses stop automatic reconnection.

Failure scenarios

Table 9.4 — SSE failure scenarios.

What goes wrong Why Detection Recovery Prevention
Events arrive in bursts minutes late Reverse proxy or compression buffers the response Server log timestamps vs. client receipt times diverge Disable buffering on the route proxy_buffering off / X-Accel-Buffering: no; no gzip on streams
Streams die every 60 s Idle timeout on LB or proxy Reconnect rate ≈ connections / 60 s Send heartbeats Comment line every 15–30 s, below every idle timeout
Clients never reconnect after outage LB returned 502/503; EventSource fails permanently on non-200 Connected-client gauge drops and stays low Application recreates EventSource with jittered backoff Handle readyState === CLOSED in onerror
Seventh tab hangs HTTP/1.1 six-connection limit per origin Requests pending in browser dev tools Close tabs Serve SSE over HTTP/2; share one stream across tabs (BroadcastChannel, SharedWorker)

Common misconceptions

“SSE is obsolete because WebSockets exist.” SSE is the better tool for one-directional streams: it rides on ordinary HTTP (so HTTP/2 multiplexing, standard authentication and observability all apply), it resumes automatically, and it needs no special proxy configuration. Choose WebSockets when the client also sends frequent low-latency messages, or when you need binary frames.

9.6 WebSockets in depth

9.6.1 What a WebSocket is

Definition — WebSocket. A protocol, standardized in RFC 6455 [Fette & Melnikov 2011], that starts as an HTTP/1.1 request, upgrades the underlying TCP connection, and thereafter carries a full-duplex sequence of framed messages in both directions with 2–14 bytes of framing overhead per frame. URLs use the schemes ws:// (plain TCP, default port 80) and wss:// (over TLS, default port 443).

First-principles explanation

HTTP is a postal system: every letter needs a full envelope, and the recipient can only reply, never write first. A WebSocket is a telephone call that begins with a short postal exchange — “may we switch to the telephone?”, “yes” — after which either party speaks whenever it likes for a few bytes of overhead. Because the call starts as a letter, it passes through the same post offices (ports 80/443, HTTP proxies).

Why does this exist?

Before RFC 6455 (2011), bidirectional browser communication meant gluing a long poll (downstream) to separate POSTs (upstream), each carrying hundreds of bytes of headers. Games, collaborative editors, trading screens and chat needed many small messages per second both ways. RFC 6455 reuses HTTP’s ports for the initial connection, keeps framing minimal, keeps the browser’s origin-based security model, and avoids giving web pages a raw TCP socket that could attack other protocols.

9.6.2 The opening handshake

How it works internally

  1. The client opens a TCP connection (and, for wss://, a TLS session) to the server.
  2. It sends an HTTP/1.1 GET with these headers:
    • Upgrade: websocket and Connection: Upgrade — ask to switch protocols.
    • Sec-WebSocket-Key: — 16 random bytes, base64-encoded, fresh for each connection.
    • Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13 — the only version in RFC 6455.
    • Origin: — set by browsers; the server must check it (see the security note below).
    • Optionally Sec-WebSocket-Protocol: (application subprotocols, for example graphql-transport-ws or mqtt) and Sec-WebSocket-Extensions: (for example permessage-deflate, RFC 7692).
  3. The server validates the request and responds HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols with Upgrade: websocket, Connection: Upgrade and Sec-WebSocket-Accept, computed as base64(SHA-1(key + 258EAFA5-E914-47DA-95CA-C5AB0DC85B11)). That fixed GUID appears in RFC 6455; the computation proves that the server actually understood a WebSocket handshake (and was not, say, an unsuspecting HTTP server or cache replaying a response). It is not an authentication mechanism.
  4. From the next byte onward, both sides speak the WebSocket framing protocol on the same TCP connection. HTTP is gone.
GET /chat HTTP/1.1
Host: server.example.com
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Key: dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==
Origin: https://example.com
Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13

HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Accept: s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo=

Cross-Site WebSocket Hijacking. Browsers attach cookies to the WebSocket handshake but WebSockets are not subject to CORS. If your server authenticates the handshake by cookie and does not check Origin against an allow-list, any website the user visits can open an authenticated WebSocket to your service. Check Origin, or authenticate with a short-lived token sent in the first message or in the URL rather than relying on cookies alone.

HTTP/2 and HTTP/3. RFC 6455’s Upgrade mechanism exists only in HTTP/1.1. RFC 8441 defines an “extended CONNECT” method that carries a WebSocket over a single HTTP/2 stream, and RFC 9220 does the same for HTTP/3; support across browsers, proxies and servers is uneven (as of 2024), so most deployments still run WebSockets over a dedicated HTTP/1.1-upgraded TCP connection.

Figure 9.4 — WebSocket opening handshake, message exchange, heartbeat and closing handshake.

Reading the diagram. One TCP connection carries the whole session. Only the upgrade request and the 101 response are HTTP; afterward frames flow independently in both directions — the server pushes a chat message unasked, the client sends a typing indicator without waiting. Client frames are masked, server frames are not (§9.6.4). Ping/Pong is a protocol-level liveness check. In the closing handshake each side sends one Close frame and the server closes TCP first, so TIME_WAIT (§7.7) accumulates on the server. Failure points: proxies that do not understand Upgrade, idle timeouts, and abrupt TCP loss with no Close frame (reported locally as 1006). The server is stateful for the connection’s lifetime, which drives §9.9.

Code example

import base64
import hashlib

GUID = "258EAFA5-E914-47DA-95CA-C5AB0DC85B11"  # fixed by RFC 6455

def accept_key(sec_websocket_key: str) -> str:
    """Compute Sec-WebSocket-Accept from the client's Sec-WebSocket-Key."""
    digest = hashlib.sha1((sec_websocket_key + GUID).encode("ascii")).digest()
    return base64.b64encode(digest).decode("ascii")

print(accept_key("dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ=="))   # s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo=

What to notice: the output matches the example in RFC 6455 exactly. SHA-1’s known collision weaknesses do not matter here because the value is a protocol-confirmation nonce, not a security signature.

9.6.3 Frames

How it works internally

After the handshake, every message is sent as one or more frames. The header is at least 2 bytes:

Table 9.5 — WebSocket frame header fields (RFC 6455 §5.2).

Field Size Meaning
FIN 1 bit 1 = this is the final fragment of a message
RSV1–3 3 bits Reserved for extensions (RSV1 marks a compressed message under permessage-deflate)
Opcode 4 bits Frame type (Table 9.6)
MASK 1 bit 1 = payload is masked; must be 1 for client→server, 0 for server→client
Payload length 7 bits 0–125 = actual length; 126 = next 2 bytes hold length; 127 = next 8 bytes hold length
Extended length 0, 2 or 8 bytes Present when length field is 126 or 127
Masking key 0 or 4 bytes Present when MASK = 1
Payload variable Application data (after unmasking)

Table 9.6 — WebSocket opcodes.

Opcode Type Notes
0x0 Continuation Subsequent fragment of a fragmented message
0x1 Text Payload must be valid UTF-8
0x2 Binary Arbitrary bytes (Protocol Buffers, MessagePack, media)
0x8 Close Optional 2-byte status code + UTF-8 reason
0x9 Ping Receiver must answer with a Pong carrying the same payload
0xA Pong Reply to Ping, or unsolicited one-way heartbeat

Control frames (Close, Ping, Pong) carry at most 125 bytes of payload, must not be fragmented, and may be injected between the fragments of a large data message — so a 100 MB upload does not delay a heartbeat. Fragmentation lets a sender stream a message of unknown length: the first frame has opcode Text or Binary with FIN = 0, middle frames use opcode Continuation, and the last frame sets FIN = 1. Note that WebSocket gives you messages, not a byte stream: the receiver’s API delivers whole messages, which is one of its key conveniences over raw TCP.

Mathematical foundations

WebSocket framing overhead per frame

H=2+Lext+4m,Lext={0n≤1252126≤n≤65,5358n≥65,536H = 2 + L_{\text{ext}} + 4m, \qquad L_{\text{ext}} = \begin{cases} 0 & n \le 125 \\ 2 & 126 \le n \le 65{,}535 \\ 8 & n \ge 65{,}536 \end{cases}

Symbol Meaning Units
HH Header bytes per frame bytes
nn Payload length bytes
LextL_{\text{ext}} Extended-length bytes bytes
mm 1 if masked (client→server), 0 otherwise dimensionless

Worked example — Sending a 60-byte chat message.

  1. Server→client: n=60≤125n = 60 \le 125, unmasked → H=2H = 2 bytes. Total 62 bytes, 3 % overhead.
  2. Client→server: masked → H=2+4=6H = 2 + 4 = 6 bytes. Total 66 bytes.
  3. The same message as an HTTP/1.1 long-poll response would carry roughly 200–800 bytes of headers — 3× to 13× the payload.
  4. TLS 1.3 with AES-GCM adds about 22 bytes per record (5-byte record header, 1-byte inner content type, 16-byte authentication tag), and TCP/IP adds 40+ bytes per packet, so for tiny messages the transport, not WebSocket, dominates.

Engineering implication. For high-frequency small messages (cursor positions, game state, typing indicators) WebSocket framing is close to free, which is why chat and multiplayer systems prefer it. To save more, batch several small updates into one frame every 50–100 ms.

Code example

The following encoder/decoder is runnable with the standard library and reproduces the byte layout from Table 9.5.

import os
import struct

def encode_frame(payload: bytes, opcode: int = 0x1, mask: bool = True) -> bytes:
    """Build a single, unfragmented frame (FIN=1)."""
    first = 0x80 | opcode                      # FIN bit + opcode
    n = len(payload)
    mask_bit = 0x80 if mask else 0x00
    if n <= 125:
        header = struct.pack("!BB", first, mask_bit | n)
    elif n <= 0xFFFF:
        header = struct.pack("!BBH", first, mask_bit | 126, n)
    else:
        header = struct.pack("!BBQ", first, mask_bit | 127, n)
    if not mask:
        return header + payload
    key = os.urandom(4)                        # fresh masking key per frame
    masked = bytes(b ^ key[i % 4] for i, b in enumerate(payload))
    return header + key + masked

def decode_frame(frame: bytes):
    """Parse one complete frame; return (fin, opcode, payload)."""
    b0, b1 = frame[0], frame[1]
    fin, opcode = bool(b0 & 0x80), b0 & 0x0F
    masked, n = bool(b1 & 0x80), b1 & 0x7F
    pos = 2
    if n == 126:
        (n,) = struct.unpack("!H", frame[pos:pos + 2]); pos += 2
    elif n == 127:
        (n,) = struct.unpack("!Q", frame[pos:pos + 8]); pos += 8
    key = b""
    if masked:
        key = frame[pos:pos + 4]; pos += 4
    data = frame[pos:pos + n]
    if masked:
        data = bytes(b ^ key[i % 4] for i, b in enumerate(data))
