BvictimB_{\text{victim}} Traffic arriving at the victim bits/s
BattackerB_{\text{attacker}} Spoofed request traffic the attacker sends bits/s
AA Bandwidth amplification factor of the abused protocol (response bytes / request bytes) dimensionless

Worked example — DNS amplification. US-CERT lists DNS amplification factors of roughly 28–54 [US-CERT TA14-017A]. An attacker with 2 Gbps of spoofing capacity and A=50A = 50 produces B=2×50=100B = 2 \times 50 = 100 Gbps at the victim. A single origin data center with a 10 Gbps uplink is saturated tenfold; nothing the origin does locally helps, because the link is full before packets reach any server. Engineering implication: volumetric defense must happen upstream, in networks whose capacity exceeds the attack — anycast CDNs and scrubbing services that advertise your IP prefixes from many locations and absorb the flood across their global capacity.

GitHub memcached attack (2018) and HTTP/2 Rapid Reset (2023). On 28 February 2018 GitHub received a 1.35 Tbps memcached-reflection attack; memcached servers exposed on UDP can amplify requests by factors in the tens of thousands. GitHub routed traffic to its DDoS-mitigation provider and the attack was mitigated within about ten minutes. In 2023 the “HTTP/2 Rapid Reset” technique (CVE-2023-44487) — opening and immediately cancelling streams on a single connection — produced application-layer floods that Google reported peaking at about 398 million requests per second. Evidence: Primary — [GitHub 2018]; [Google Cloud 2023]

Figure 10.9 — DDoS mitigation in layers.

Reading the diagram. Traffic flows left to right through successively narrower and more expensive layers. The anycast edge, spread across many locations, absorbs volumetric and protocol floods (the scrubbing stage) because its aggregate capacity is far larger than any single origin’s. The CDN serves cacheable content without touching the origin and applies L7 controls: WAF rules, per-IP and per-session rate limits, and bot challenges. The origin should accept traffic only from the edge (allow-list the CDN’s ranges or use authenticated origin pulls), otherwise attackers bypass the edge by hitting the origin IP directly. Inside, the load balancer defends connection state, and the application enforces per-user quotas and sheds load (§22.9) so that the database — the scarcest resource — sees bounded concurrency. Scaling: autoscaling helps against L7 floods only up to your budget; an attacker’s marginal cost per request is usually lower than yours, so the main lever is making requests cheap (caching) or refusing them early.

Design rules. Put every public endpoint behind an anycast CDN or DDoS-protection service; hide origin IPs; cache aggressively; make expensive endpoints (search, report generation, login) authenticated and rate-limited; set timeouts and bounded queues everywhere (§22.11); know in advance who you call and what you toggle during an attack (a runbook, rehearsed).

10.12 Audit logging and tamper evidence

Definition — Audit log. An append-only record of security-relevant events — who (actor), did what (action), to which resource, when, from where, and with what result — retained so that actions can be investigated and attributed. A log is tamper-evident if any modification, deletion or reordering of past entries can be detected.

First-principles explanation

An audit log is a bank’s bound, page-numbered ledger written in ink: you can add lines but cannot tear out a page or erase a line without it being obvious. Application debug logs are the opposite — a whiteboard. Attackers who gain privileged access routinely delete or edit logs to hide their tracks, and malicious insiders are precisely the people with access to logs. So audit logs must be designed so that the people being audited cannot rewrite them.

What to log. Authentication events (success, failure, MFA changes), authorization failures, privilege and role changes, access to sensitive data (reads, exports), administrative and configuration changes, key and secret usage (KMS logs this for you), and security-control changes (disabling logging is itself an event). Each entry: timestamp (UTC, synchronized clock), actor identity (user and workload), source (IP, device), action, resource, result, and a request or trace ID. What not to log: passwords, session tokens, full card numbers, secret values, or more personal data than necessary — the log becomes a sensitive data store itself.

How tamper evidence works. Each entry includes the hash of the previous entry, forming a hash chain: hi=H(hi−1∥ei)h_i = H(h_{i-1} \,\|\, e_i). Changing any past entry changes its hash and breaks every link after it. A chain alone is not enough — whoever can write the log can recompute the whole chain — so the latest hash (the head) is periodically anchored somewhere the writer cannot alter: signed by a key in a KMS, written to a separate account’s write-once (WORM) storage, or published to an external transparency log. Schneier and Kelsey described keyed hash-chain audit logs in 1999; Crosby and Wallach later showed how Merkle-tree structures make such logs efficiently verifiable — the same idea behind Certificate Transparency (§10.5) [Schneier & Kelsey 1999; Crosby & Wallach 2009].

Figure 10.10 — Tamper-evident audit logging pipeline.

Reading the diagram. Services emit events asynchronously to a stream (dotted arrows), so logging never blocks user requests — at the cost that events can be delayed; the stream must be durable so events are not lost. A single writer appends each event with the previous entry’s hash. Every hour it asks the KMS to sign the current head (the signing key is usable only by the writer’s role and never leaves the KMS) and stores signed heads and log replicas in a WORM bucket in a separate account with object lock, so even production administrators cannot delete them before retention expires. An independent verifier recomputes the chain and compares it with the signed heads, alerting the security team on any mismatch. Failure points: the writer is a bottleneck and single point of ordering (partition the chain per service or per tenant to scale); clock skew complicates ordering (use the chain order, not timestamps, as the authority).

"""Tamper-evident audit log: each entry commits to the previous one (hash chain)."""
import hashlib
import hmac
import json

GENESIS = "0" * 64

def entry_hash(prev_hash: str, event: dict) -> str:
    payload = json.dumps(event, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":")).encode()
    return hashlib.sha256(prev_hash.encode() + payload).hexdigest()

class AuditLog:
    def __init__(self):
        self.entries: list[dict] = []

    def append(self, event: dict) -> str:
        prev = self.entries[-1]["hash"] if self.entries else GENESIS
        h = entry_hash(prev, event)
        self.entries.append({"event": event, "prev": prev, "hash": h})
        return h                       # publish/anchor this "head" externally

    def verify(self, anchored_head: str | None = None) -> int | None:
        """Return index of first bad entry, or None if the chain is intact."""
        prev = GENESIS
        for i, e in enumerate(self.entries):
            if e["prev"] != prev or not hmac.compare_digest(e["hash"], entry_hash(prev, e["event"])):
                return i
            prev = e["hash"]
        if anchored_head is not None and prev != anchored_head:
            return len(self.entries)   # tail truncated or rewritten
        return None

Tested: an intact chain verifies; editing the resource field of entry 1 makes verify return index 1; deleting the last entry is caught only when the verifier is given the previously anchored head.

What to notice: canonical JSON (sort_keys, fixed separators) makes the hash reproducible; truncation is detectable only because the verifier holds an anchored head from outside the log; and in production the anchor is signed and stored where the writer cannot overwrite it.

AWS CloudTrail log file integrity validation. CloudTrail delivers hourly digest files that contain the SHA-256 hashes of the log files delivered in that hour, are signed with an RSA key held by AWS, and include the signature of the previous digest — a signed hash chain. Customers verify with a CLI command and are advised to store logs in a separate account with S3 Object Lock. Evidence: Primary — [AWS Docs: CloudTrail log file integrity validation]

10.13 A security checklist for every design

Use this table in every design document and design review — and in interviews, where spending two minutes on it distinguishes senior candidates.

Table 10.13 — Security checklist for every design.

Area Question to answer in the design Default good answer Section
Threat model What are the assets, adversaries and trust boundaries? Top 3 threats? DFD with boundaries; STRIDE table; owners for mitigations §10.3
Authentication How is every user and every service identified? Central IdP, MFA for humans; mTLS or signed tokens for services §10.10, §8.11
Authorization Where is each access decision made? Default? Deny by default; central policy; object-level checks in data layer §10.7.1
Input handling What untrusted input crosses boundaries, and how is it validated? Schema validation; parameterized queries; output encoding; SSRF egress proxy §10.7
Data in transit Is every hop encrypted, including internal ones? TLS 1.3 everywhere; mTLS between services §10.4.4, §10.10
Data at rest What is sensitive? At which layer is it encrypted? Who can decrypt? Volume encryption everywhere; KMS envelope/field encryption for sensitive fields §10.9
Keys and secrets Where do secrets live? Lifetime? Rotation? Vault or KMS; short-lived dynamic credentials; no secrets in code or images §10.8
Passwords If you store them, how? Argon2id (or scrypt/bcrypt), unique salt, optional pepper, breached-list check §10.6
Least privilege What is the minimum each component can do? Blast radius if compromised? Per-service roles; segmented networks; no standing admin access §10.10.3
Availability under attack What happens under a 100× traffic flood? CDN/anycast, rate limits, quotas, load shedding, hidden origin §10.11
Logging and detection Can you reconstruct who did what? Can logs be altered? Structured audit log; tamper-evident; separate account; alerts §10.12
Supply chain How do dependencies and builds stay trustworthy? Pinned dependencies, scanning, signed artifacts, protected CI §10.7, Ch 50
Incident response Who is paged, what is revoked, how do you rotate everything? Runbooks; tested key rotation; backups that attackers cannot delete §39.12
Privacy and retention Do you need this data? For how long? Collect minimum; retention limits; crypto-shredding for deletion §10.9, Ch 50

10.14 Summary and revision notes

  • Security is a property of the architecture. Ask “against whom, protecting what, for which property (CIA, authentication, authorization, non-repudiation)?”
  • Threat modeling: draw a DFD, mark trust boundaries, walk STRIDE per element, rank with likelihood × impact, and turn mitigations into tracked requirements. Most mitigations are architectural.
  • Pick primitives by goal: hash (fingerprint, no key), MAC (shared-key authenticity), AEAD such as AES-GCM (secrecy + integrity), asymmetric encryption/KEM (no pre-shared key), signatures (publicly verifiable, non-repudiation), ECDHE (key agreement with forward secrecy), CSPRNG (all randomness).
  • Never reuse a GCM nonce with the same key; never use H(key‖msg) as a MAC; never compare MACs with ==; never use MD5/SHA-1 for security; use high-level libraries.
  • PKI binds keys to names through CA signatures; Certificate Transparency makes mis-issuance detectable; short-lived, automatically rotated certificates beat revocation.
  • Passwords: Argon2id (OWASP minimum m = 19 MiB, t = 2, p = 1), scrypt or bcrypt; unique salt; optional pepper in a KMS; store parameters; rehash on login; check breached lists; MFA. Expected cracking time T=S/(2RG)T = S / (2RG).
  • OWASP Top 10 categories are missing central controls: deny-by-default authorization, parameterized queries, egress proxies against SSRF, signed artifacts, audit logging.
  • Secrets: vault, short-lived dynamic credentials, workload identity, two-version rotation, secret scanning. Misuse window shrinks from months to the TTL.
  • Encrypt in transit everywhere (TLS 1.3, mTLS). At rest, the layer decides which attacker you stop. Envelope encryption: DEK encrypts data locally, KMS-held KEK wraps the DEK; cheap rotation, auditable decrypts, crypto-shredding.
  • Zero trust: no trust from network location; per-request authentication and authorization of user, device and workload (BeyondCorp, NIST SP 800-207), plus least privilege and segmentation for defense in depth.
  • DDoS: volumetric (bandwidth, absorb upstream), protocol (state, SYN cookies/stateless edge), application (requests, rate limits, caching, shedding). Amplification Bvictim=Battacker×AB_{\text{victim}} = B_{\text{attacker}} \times A.
  • Audit logs: who/what/which/when/where/result, no secrets; hash-chained, anchored heads signed and stored in WORM storage outside the writer’s control.

10.15 Knowledge checkpoint

  1. Which STRIDE category does each of the following violate: (a) a forged webhook, (b) an admin denying a deletion, (c) reading another user’s invoice by changing an ID?
  2. Why is SHA-256(key∥message)\text{SHA-256}(\text{key} \,\|\, \text{message}) not a safe MAC, and what does HMAC change?
  3. What happens if AES-GCM encrypts two messages with the same key and nonce?
  4. What is the purpose of associated data (AAD) in an AEAD scheme? Give a database example.
  5. Why does TLS 1.3 use ephemeral Diffie–Hellman rather than RSA key transport?
  6. A MAC and a signature both detect tampering. Which one provides non-repudiation, and why?
  7. What problem does Certificate Transparency solve that the CA chain alone does not?
  8. Name three reasons salts are required in password storage.
  9. Compute the entropy of a 10-character password chosen uniformly from 62 alphanumeric characters.
  10. Give two architectural controls for SSRF beyond URL validation.
  11. Classify: SYN flood, DNS amplification, HTTP flood on /search.
  12. Why must the head of a hash-chained audit log be anchored outside the log?
Answers
    1. Spoofing; (b) Repudiation; (c) Elevation of privilege (an authorization failure — an IDOR; it also causes information disclosure).
  2. SHA-256 is vulnerable to length extension: from the tag of key‖m, an attacker can compute a valid tag for key‖m‖padding‖x without the key. HMAC’s nested two-pass construction with inner and outer padded keys prevents this.
  3. The same keystream is used twice, so XORing the ciphertexts reveals the XOR of the plaintexts, and the authentication key can be recovered, enabling forgeries. Confidentiality and integrity both fail.
  4. AAD is authenticated but not encrypted; it binds ciphertext to its context. Putting table=users;id=42 in the AAD prevents an attacker with DB write access from moving that ciphertext to row 43.
  5. Forward secrecy: ephemeral keys are discarded after each session, so stealing the server’s long-term key later does not decrypt recorded traffic. The long-term key only signs.
  6. The signature. A MAC key is shared by both parties, so either could have produced the tag; only the private-key holder can produce a signature, and anyone can verify it.
  7. It detects a trusted CA issuing a certificate for your domain to someone else (compromise or error). The chain only shows some trusted CA signed it; CT logs make every issuance public so domain owners can notice.
  8. Identical passwords no longer have identical hashes; precomputed (rainbow) tables become useless; attackers must attack each user separately, multiplying cost by the number of users.
  9. H=10×log262≈10×5.954=59.5H = 10 \times \log_2 62 \approx 10 \times 5.954 = 59.5 bits.
  10. A dedicated egress proxy in a network segment without routes to internal ranges; blocking or token-protecting the metadata service (IMDSv2); least-privilege instance roles; pinning resolved IPs and disabling redirects.
  11. SYN flood: protocol (state exhaustion). DNS amplification: volumetric. HTTP flood on /search: application layer.
  12. Anyone who can write the log can recompute the entire chain after editing it. A head signed by a separate key and stored in WORM storage the writer cannot modify fixes a point the rewritten chain will not match.

10.16 Interview questions

Basic

Q1. How should a web application store user passwords? Answer. Never in plaintext or reversibly encrypted. Hash each password with a slow, memory-hard password-hashing function — Argon2id by default (at least m = 19 MiB, t = 2, p = 1 per OWASP), otherwise scrypt or bcrypt — with a unique random salt of at least 16 bytes. Store algorithm and parameters with the hash so you can raise cost later and rehash on next login. Optionally apply a pepper (a secret key in a KMS/HSM) so a database-only leak is not attackable. Compare in constant time, rate-limit login, check new passwords against breached lists, and offer MFA. Size the login fleet for the hashing cost.

Q2. What is the difference between encryption, hashing and signing? Answer. Encryption provides confidentiality and is reversible with a key. Hashing is a keyless one-way fingerprint for integrity against a trusted reference. Signing uses a private key to produce a tag anyone can verify with the public key, providing integrity, authenticity and non-repudiation. A MAC is the shared-key analog of a signature without non-repudiation. AEAD encryption combines confidentiality with integrity.

Intermediate

Q3. Design encryption for a multi-tenant document store where each tenant’s data must be deletable on request, including from backups. Answer. Use envelope encryption with a per-tenant KEK in a KMS and a per-document DEK. Each document is encrypted locally with AES-256-GCM under its DEK; the wrapped DEK and KEK ID are stored with it, and the encryption context includes tenant ID and document ID. IAM policy on each KEK allows decrypt only by the service’s role, and KMS logs every decrypt for audit. To delete a tenant, schedule deletion of its KEK: all its DEKs, and therefore all copies of its documents including immutable backups, become unreadable (crypto-shredding). Discuss KMS quotas (DEK per document is fine for large documents; batch keys for tiny records), KMS availability as a dependency, regional keys for residency, and the waiting period that protects against accidental KEK deletion.

Q4. A partner sends you webhooks. How do you make sure they are genuine and not replayed? Answer. Share a high-entropy secret per partner (with a key ID for rotation). The partner computes HMAC-SHA-256 over a canonical string of timestamp, a unique event ID or nonce, and the raw body. You verify by recomputing over the raw bytes, comparing in constant time, rejecting timestamps outside a ±5-minute window and rejecting event IDs already seen (a shared store with TTL just longer than the window). Process idempotently by event ID (§22.15), since retries are legitimate. Support two active keys during rotation. Use TLS for confidentiality; HMAC provides authenticity.

Advanced

Q5. Your company runs 400 microservices on a flat internal network with shared database passwords in environment variables. Propose a two-year security roadmap. Answer. Start with visibility: inventory services and data flows, threat-model the most sensitive data stores, centralize tamper-evident audit logging. Phase 1 (0–6 months): move secrets into a vault and rotate all of them (assume compromise); add secret scanning; one IAM role and one database user per service. Phase 2 (6–12 months): issue short-lived SPIFFE-style workload certificates via a mesh or library; enable mTLS in permissive then strict mode; move databases to dynamic credentials. Phase 3 (12–24 months): default-deny network policies, per-service authorization policies, an identity-aware proxy for internal tools, just-in-time admin access. Measure progress (share of traffic on mTLS, secrets older than 30 days, wildcard permissions), roll out with dashboards and per-phase rollback switches. Trade-offs: mesh latency and operational load, database connection limits with per-workload users, and the need for owned, reviewed policies.

Q6. How would you design an audit logging system for a bank that regulators and internal investigators must be able to trust, even against a malicious administrator? Answer. Define the event schema (actor, workload, action, resource, result, source, trace ID) and emit from every service through a durable stream so logging does not block requests. A writer service builds per-partition hash chains; hourly it signs each chain head using a KMS key restricted to the writer role and writes signed heads plus log segments to WORM storage (object lock in compliance mode) in a separate account administered by a different team. An independent verifier recomputes chains and compares with signed heads; mismatches alert security operations. Separate duties: no single administrator controls the production account, the log account and the KMS key policy. Index a copy in a SIEM for search, treating the SIEM as derived and untrusted. Address clock sync, retention (years, per regulation), personal data minimization, and Merkle-tree structures if third parties need efficient inclusion proofs.

10.17 Practical exercises

  1. Password hashing benchmark. Run the code in §10.6.2. Increase Argon2id memory to 64 MiB and tt to 3 and measure latency. Compute how many cores you would need for 500 logins per second at peak with 50% headroom.
  2. HMAC request signing. Extend the code in §10.4.6 to support two active keys per client, and write a test proving that removing the HTTP method from the canonical string lets an attacker turn a signed GET into a DELETE.
  3. Envelope encryption. Extend the FakeKMS example in §10.9.2 with a per-tenant KEK and a delete_tenant operation. Show that encrypted objects for a deleted tenant can no longer be decrypted while other tenants are unaffected. Then replace FakeKMS with a real KMS client in a sandbox account if you have one.
  4. Brute-force calculator. Write a function that takes alphabet size, length, guesses per second and number of GPUs and prints expected time. Use it to compare a 4-word and a 6-word Diceware passphrase (7,776 words) against bcrypt and against unsalted SHA-256.
  5. Tamper-evident log. Modify the audit log in §10.12 so that every 100 entries the head is signed with an Ed25519 key (§10.4.8). Write a verifier that accepts only chains whose signed heads verify.
  6. Threat model. Draw a DFD for a URL shortener (§52.1) with trust boundaries and produce a STRIDE table with at least eight threats ranked by L×IL \times I.

10.18 Design challenges

  1. Secure file-sharing link service. Users share files by link; links can expire and be revoked; recipients may be anonymous. Design storage encryption, link-token generation (entropy and length), revocation, download rate limiting and audit logging. Identify where signed URLs, HMAC and envelope encryption each fit.
  2. Zero-trust migration for an admin console. A company’s internal admin console is reachable over VPN by 300 support agents and offers “view any customer” functionality. Redesign access with an identity-aware proxy, device posture, just-in-time elevation for sensitive actions and an audit trail that customers can be shown. State the failure mode if the identity provider is down.
  3. DDoS-resilient public API. A public API serves 20,000 RPS normally, with an expensive search endpoint costing 50 ms of database time per request. Design layered defenses for a 1 Tbps volumetric attack and for a 2 million RPS application-layer flood from residential IPs. Quantify how much the cache hit ratio and per-key rate limits reduce database load.

Appendix E — Learning Roadmap and Proficiency Levels

Deliverable 3. This appendix turns the 93 chapters into a schedule. It defines five proficiency levels, what you must know and be able to do at each, and week-by-week milestones for three tracks: the full 12-month program, a 16-week interview track, and a 24-week ML/AI infrastructure track for working engineers.

E.1 How to use this roadmap

  1. Find your starting level with the self-assessment in §E.3. Do not skip a level because a topic “sounds familiar” — the readiness criteria test whether you can explain and apply a concept, not whether you recognize its name.
  2. Pick a track (§E.4–E.6). Each week lists chapters, a hands-on task and a checkpoint. Budget the stated hours; if a week overruns, extend it rather than skipping the exercise — implementation is where understanding consolidates (Ch 3, §3.7).
  3. At the end of every month, run the month’s milestone review: answer the knowledge checkpoints of each chapter from memory, redraw the month’s key architecture diagrams without notes, and solve one design challenge aloud in 45 minutes.
  4. Record progress in a design journal (template in Ch 3, §3.10).

Level 1 — Absolute beginner

Dimension Definition
Required knowledge Ch 1–8, 11, 35. What a client, server, API, database, process, thread, IP address, DNS lookup and HTTP request are; functional vs non-functional requirements; powers of ten and basic percentiles.
Expected competencies Trace one HTTP request from browser to database and back, naming every hop. Write a CRUD REST API with a relational database. Model a simple domain in tables with primary/foreign keys. Do a back-of-the-envelope estimate of requests per second from daily active users.

Architecture exercises Draw a single-server web app; then add a load balancer and a second app server and explain what breaks (sessions).
Interview readiness Not yet ready for system design rounds. Can answer “what happens when you type a URL?” thoroughly.
Explain independently TCP vs UDP; what an index is and why it speeds reads but slows writes; what latency vs throughput mean; why HTTPS needs certificates.

Level 2 — Intermediate engineer

Dimension Definition
Required knowledge Ch 9–10, 12, 14, 17–22, 24, 30, 33, 36–37, 57. Replication, sharding, consistent hashing, caching patterns, CDNs, load-balancing algorithms, rate limiting, queues and pub/sub, monolith vs microservices, ML basics.
Expected competencies Turn a vague prompt into numbered FRs/NFRs with targets. Estimate storage, bandwidth and RPS with peak factors. Choose SQL vs NoSQL with justification. Add a cache and explain invalidation and stampede protection. Design a rate limiter and pick an algorithm.
Practical projects P-03 Redis cache; P-04 rate limiter; P-05 load-balancer simulation; P-06 message queue.
Architecture exercises URL shortener, Pastebin, rate limiter and notification system (Ch 52) at 10⁷ DAU.
Interview readiness Can complete an entry-level (new-grad / mid-level) system design round: correct high-level architecture, reasonable estimates, identifies the main bottleneck.
Explain independently Cache-aside vs write-through; why sharding needs a good key; at-least-once delivery and why consumers must be idempotent; Little’s Law applied to a thread pool.

Level 3 — Advanced engineer

Dimension Definition
Required knowledge Ch 13, 15–16, 23, 25–27, 29, 31–32, 34, 38–43, 58–62, 66. Storage engines, consistency models, Raft, quorums, Kafka internals, outbox/saga/CQRS, observability, Kubernetes, CI/CD, ML lifecycle, feature stores, model serving.
Expected competencies Design a complete distributed application with explicit consistency choices, failure handling and observability. Explain a database’s write path down to WAL and fsync. Design an ML system from problem formulation to online serving with a feature store.
Practical projects P-07 distributed KV store; P-08 replicated DB simulation; P-09 notification service; P-10 real-time chat; P-11 distributed job scheduler.
Architecture exercises All of Ch 52–53; ML case studies 81.5 (product recommendation) and 82.3 (spam detection).
Interview readiness Passes a senior-level (L5/E5 equivalent) traditional round and a mid-level ML system design round: deep-dives on request, quantifies trade-offs, discusses failure modes unprompted.
Explain independently Raft leader election and log matching; why R + W > N gives read-your-writes only under certain conditions; Kafka ISR and acks=all; point-in-time feature joins and training–serving skew.

Level 4 — Senior / Staff engineer

Dimension Definition
Required knowledge Ch 28, 44, 46–48, 50–51, 63–65, 67–80. Distributed transactions, multi-region design, cluster scheduling, multi-tenancy, security architecture, cost; GPU performance, distributed training, model optimization, recommendation architecture, MLOps, LLM inference, RAG, agents, AI platforms.
Expected competencies Make and defend architecture decisions spanning teams: multi-region active–active, tenant isolation, SLOs and error budgets, cost models. Size a GPU fleet for training and for LLM serving from first principles. Design a RAG or agent platform with evaluation, guardrails and observability.
Practical projects P-12 event-driven microservices; P-13 real-time analytics pipeline; P-14 recommendation engine; P-15 distributed ML inference; P-18 production RAG; P-19 scalable LLM inference.
Architecture exercises All of Ch 54–56 and 81–86. Write a design document with ADRs for one case study and have it reviewed.
Interview readiness Passes staff-level rounds: drives the conversation, scopes ambiguity, prioritizes the hardest sub-problem, connects technical choices to business, cost and organizational constraints.
Explain independently Spanner commit-wait; why cells limit blast radius; ZeRO stage 3 memory math; continuous batching and PagedAttention; when RAG beats fine-tuning; how to evaluate an agent.

Level 5 — Expert / Principal architect

Dimension Definition
Required knowledge Ch 45, 49, 80 plus the primary papers cited across Parts V, IX, XIII and XVI. Theory (FLP, CAP proofs, BFT bounds, consistency hierarchies, scaling laws) and practice at 10⁴–10⁵ machine scale.
Expected competencies Set multi-year technical direction; evaluate novel systems from papers; reason about organization-wide failure domains, reliability economics and sustainability; design platforms other teams build on.
Practical projects P-16 distributed training platform; P-17 multi-tenant feature store; P-20 multi-agent orchestration platform.
Architecture exercises Critique a published architecture (e.g., a Dynamo, Spanner or PagedAttention paper) and propose a design for a changed constraint. Lead a postmortem-driven redesign.
Interview readiness Principal-level: articulates long-term trade-offs, migration strategy, organizational design (Conway’s law), and the economics of the platform.
Explain independently Why consensus is impossible in a fully asynchronous system with one crash failure and how real systems sidestep it; goodput at 16k-GPU scale; the cost/latency frontier of an LLM product.
